bio.en: Gustav Söderström is co-president, chief product officer, and chief technology officer at Spotify, where he oversees the company's global product and technology strategy across product, design, data, and engineering.
bio.zh: Gustav Söderström 是 Spotify 的联合总裁、首席产品官兼首席技术官，负责公司在产品、设计、数据与工程领域的全球产品与技术战略。

summary.en: Gustav frames the internet's evolution as curation → recommendation → generation, arguing generative AI will force a rethink of products as profound as the shift to recommendation did. He shares what he's learned about placing big bets and what to do when they fail, how Spotify moved away from squads to its current team structure, and how AI is already reshaping Spotify's product and the future of AI-generated music. He also explains why every great product must pull a 'magic trick,' and offers a memorable (and hilarious) analogy about Swedish business culture.
summary.zh: Gustav 把互联网的演进概括为“策展 → 推荐 → 生成”，主张生成式 AI 将迫使产品被重新设想，其深远程度不亚于当年转向推荐。他分享了关于下大赌注、以及赌注失败该如何应对的经验；Spotify 如何放弃 squad 模式、转向如今的团队结构；AI 已如何重塑 Spotify 的产品与 AI 生成音乐的未来。他还解释了为何每一款伟大的产品都必须耍一个“魔术”，并用一个令人难忘（且好笑）的类比谈了瑞典商业文化。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: The internet started with curation, often user curation. So you took something, some good like people or books or music, and you digitize it and you put it online and then you ask users to curate it. And that was your Facebook, Spotify, and so forth. And then after a while, the world switched from curation to recommendation, where instead of people doing that work, you had algorithms. And that was a big change that required us and others to actually rethink the entire user experience and sometimes the business model as well. And I think what we're entering now is we're going from your curation to recommendation to generation. And I suspect it will be as big of a shift that you will eventually have to rethink your products. We have to rethink the user interface and the experience for recommendation first era. And so what does that mean in the generative era? No one really knows yet.
turns.zh: 互联网最初是以内容筛选（curation）为起点的，这通常是由用户完成的。比如，你会选取一些优秀的资源——比如人脉、书籍、音乐等，将其数字化并上传至网络，然后邀请用户对这些内容进行筛选。这就是Facebook、Spotify等平台的诞生逻辑。然而，随着时间推移，世界从内容筛选转向了推荐机制——不再由人工完成筛选工作，而是由算法接管。这是一次重大变革，迫使我们和其他平台不得不重新思考整个用户体验，甚至重新审视商业模式。我认为，当前我们正经历从内容筛选到推荐，再到内容生成的转变。我相信这将带来同样重大的变革，最终你们不得不重新构思自己的产品。在推荐时代，我们需要重新设计用户界面和体验。那么，在生成内容时代，这意味着什么？目前还没有人能给出明确答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Gustav, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 古斯塔夫，欢迎做客我们的播客节目。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny. Pleasure to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀请我，莱尼。很高兴能来这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's my pleasure to have you on. So at this point, you've been at Spotify for over 14 years, which is a rare feat in the tech world, and you've held a lot of different roles while you've been at Spotify. Can you just start off by giving us a sense of what these various roles and what you've done over the years at Spotify and then just what are you up to these days? What are you responsible for now?
turns.zh: 很高兴您能参与我们的访谈。您在Spotify工作已超过14年，这在科技界实属难得。在此期间，您在Spotify担任过诸多不同职位，能否先向我们简要介绍一下这些职位，以及您在Spotify多年来的工作经历？目前您的主要职责是什么？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So I came into Spotify in early 2009, late 2008. And my job then, I had been an entrepreneur, started some of my own companies in the, back then, very, very early feature phone, smartphone space. So I had a bunch of knowledge there. I had sold the company to Yahoo in the mobile space. I worked there for a while. I came back to Sweden and then I met through a mutual friend, Daniel Ek, the CEO and co-founder of Spotify. And they had built the desktop product already, the free streaming desktop product, and it was amazing and I could try it, but they needed someone to figure out what to do with mobile. And because I had been an entrepreneur in that space, I got that job.
turns.zh: 于是我在2009年初，也就是2008年末，加入了Spotify。当时我的工作经历是，曾作为创业者，创办过几家公司，专注于当时还处于起步阶段的功能手机和智能手机领域。在移动领域，我曾将公司出售给雅虎，并在那里工作了一段时间。之后我回到瑞典，通过一位共同的朋友结识了Spotify的首席执行官兼联合创始人丹尼尔·埃克（Daniel Ek）。当时他们已经开发出了桌面版免费流媒体产品，体验非常棒，我有机会试用了一下。但他们急需有人来规划移动端的业务方向。正因我在该领域有过创业经验，我才获得了这份工作机会。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So my job was to head up mobile for Spotify and figure out what the mobile offering would be, which was a challenge because, obviously, Spotify desktop was a free on-demand streaming application and back then, specifically with edge networks, you couldn't really stream at all in real time. The performance wasn't there and also you couldn't fund that with an ads model. So it was a product and business model innovation that was a lot of fun. So that's how I started. Then after a few years, I took on all of product development for Spotify. And then a few years later, I actually took on the technology responsibility, the CTO role for Spotify as well. And recently, my official title is co-president of Spotify together with Alex Nordstrom. So we run half of the company each. I run the product and technology side and he runs for the business and content side. So that's the super fast version.
turns.zh:
当时我的任务是负责Spotify的移动端业务，构思移动产品的形态。这确实是个挑战，因为Spotify的桌面版是免费的点播流媒体应用，而当时的边缘网络技术根本无法实现实时流媒体播放。网络性能不足，且无法通过广告模式盈利。这是一次极具挑战性的产品与商业模式创新之旅。这就是我职业生涯的起点。

几年后，我接手了Spotify的全部产品开发工作。再往后几年，又担起了技术重任，出任Spotify的首席技术官。最近，我的正式头衔是Spotify联合总裁，与亚历克斯·诺德斯特伦共同管理公司事务。我们各执一半权力——我负责产品与技术板块，他则主导商业与内容业务。这就是简略版的职业历程。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Aside from getting more responsibilities taking on the technology department, it has been the same job by title. I've always reported to Daniel, but because Spotify's grown so much every six to 12 months, it's been starting at a new company. First, it was sort of a Swedish Nordic challenge and then it was a European challenge and then it was getting into the US and then we became a public company. So it's as if I had jumped around between a lot of jobs actually, even though it was largely the same title and role.
turns.zh: 除了在技术部门承担了更多职责外，我的职位名称始终如一。我一直向丹尼尔汇报工作，但由于Spotify每隔6到12个月就会迎来一次重大发展，每次都像是在创办一家新公司。最初是瑞典北欧市场的挑战，接着是欧洲市场的拓展，之后是进军美国市场，再后来我们成功上市。所以尽管职位和职责大体相同，但实际上我就像是在不同岗位之间频繁跳槽。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Your story makes me think of the classic be careful what you're good at because you end up taking on more and more. And clearly, you've been given more and more responsibility over the years and so clearly things are going well and you're doing well.
turns.zh: 你的故事让我想起那句经典名言——"小心别在自己擅长的领域钻得太深，否则最终会承担越来越多的责任。"显然，这些年你承担的责任越来越多，事情进展得也越来越顺利，你做得很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shifting a little bit. So you're on my podcast currently. You actually have your own podcast, which was this limited series on the product story of Spotify, which I listened to and loved, and it's surreal to listen to your voice in real time because I've been listening to that recently in preparation for this conversation. Two questions, just what made you decide to launch your own podcast knowing you had a full-time job and a lot going on and the production value for your podcast was very high for what I could tell? And then two, just what did you learn from that experience in terms of the product you ended up a building and just empathizing with the podcast creator side of?
turns.zh: 稍微换个话题。您现在正在参加我的播客节目。您其实自己也有一个播客，那个关于Spotify产品故事的限定系列节目，我听过而且很喜欢。现在实时听到您的声音感觉特别奇妙，因为我最近为了准备这次对话，又重新听了一遍。两个问题：第一，您当时是全职工作，事务繁忙，为什么还是决定推出自己的播客？据我所知，您播客的制作水准非常高；第二，您从这次经历中学到了什么，对您后来开发的产品有何启发？特别是对播客创作者的角度而言，您又有了哪些感悟？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: There were a bunch of different reasons why I did that. One is, and not a small one, I think, like you, I love writing and I have this secret creator dream in me. I used to write blog posts a long time ago and I write internally a lot. You can't write that much externally when you work at a company like this.
turns.zh: 我这么做的原因有很多。其中一个很重要的原因是，我和你们一样热爱写作，内心深处怀揣着成为创作者的梦想。很久以前我曾写过博客文章，现在也经常在公司内部撰写文案。但在这样的公司工作时，很难有机会进行大量对外创作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: But I love writing and talking and presenting. So there was certainly that. And then no small part was, from a product point of view, to empathize with one of our main constituents, the podcast creator. I'm, unfortunately, not a great musician. I try to play instruments and so forth, but I don't have any records. I don't sing very well. But I decided to make a podcast and that taught me a huge amount about what it's like to be a creator, creating different styles of podcast.
turns.zh: 但我热爱写作、演讲和主持节目。当然，这其中也包含了这些元素。另外，从产品角度来看，我这样做还有一个重要原因——那就是要设身处地为我们的主要用户群体——播客创作者着想。遗憾的是，我算不上出色的音乐家。我曾尝试学习乐器之类的，但从未录制过专辑，唱歌水平也不算出色。不过，我决定制作播客，这段经历让我深刻体会到成为一名创作者意味着什么，以及如何打造不同风格的播客节目。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: For example, we wanted to do a higher production cost podcast with music and then right away you run into a bunch of problems as Spotify is actually pretty well positioned to solve, but still, it's really hard to have music in a podcast from a rights perspective. So you understand all these problems that podcasters have and you can be better at solving them. But the biggest benefit and the real reason for doing the public podcast was that I have actually done an internal podcast through a hack where we could gate the podcast-only employees. And I tried to figure out internally how to build more culture around Spotify and help define for new employees and existing employees, who we are, the mistakes we did, the successes we had, and how we think about strategy specifically in product strategy because we were quite well known externally for technology and the squads and all of these things, not so much for product strategy.
turns.zh: 比如，我们想制作一期制作成本较高的播客，加入音乐元素，但随即就遇到了许多问题。虽然Spotify在版权方面本可以提供有效解决方案，但从版权角度考虑，播客中使用音乐确实存在诸多难题。正因如此，你深知播客创作者面临的这些挑战，也更善于解决这些问题。但制作这档公开播客的最大益处——以及我选择这样做的根本原因——在于我曾通过内部黑客技术手段打造过一档仅限员工收听的播客。当时我们通过技术手段将播客内容限制在内部员工访问范围内，尝试在公司内部构建更深厚的文化氛围，向新员工和现有员工清晰传递我们的企业价值观，分享成功经验与失败教训，特别是从产品战略层面进行深度解析。要知道，外界对我们最熟悉的标签是技术、敏捷团队等，而产品战略方面却鲜少被提及。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And because I love storytelling more than Google Docs, I decided to do an internal podcast and I went around and I interviewed actually Daniel's direct reports. So the CMO, the CHRO and CFO. And just ask them about a bunch of stuff. And the idea was to make them more approachable for employees because I felt listening to podcasts, even these people that have no idea who I am because I've never met them, I feel like I know them, I feel like I know how they think and I just like them much more. So the secret idea was, what if you could get to know your leaders much better than you do through occasional meetings or some town hall? So I did that internally, and because I'm a product person, we ended up talking a lot about product and product strategy. And people internally really like that.
turns.zh: 正因为我比起谷歌文档更热爱讲故事，我决定在公司内部推出一档播客节目。我走访了各部门，采访了丹尼尔的直属下属——首席营销官、首席人力资源官和首席财务官，询问了他们诸多问题。我希望借此让员工们更容易亲近这些高管，因为我发现听播客时，即便听众对这些人一无所知（毕竟我从未与他们谋面），也会产生熟悉感，能了解他们的思维方式，从而对他们好感倍增。所以我的核心构想是——如果能通过播客节目，比偶尔的会议或全体员工大会更深入地了解领导团队，那会怎样呢？于是我内部推出了这档播客。作为产品经理出身，我们最终聊得最多的是产品和产品战略。内部员工对此反响热烈。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So next time, the question was, what if people that don't even work at Spotify yet could feel as if they knew people at Spotify? That'd be great because most leaders in most companies are very opaque and appear as some otherworldly creatures that aren't really real, I think, when you see them in business papers or something. So what if you have heard them talk for an hour or so? So that was general idea. So a combination of recruitment tool, sharing more about how we think about product strategy and just because I think it was a lot of fun. I got to interview a bunch of smart and interesting people both externally and internally.
turns.zh: 接下来要考虑的是，如果那些甚至还没加入Spotify的人也能感觉自己认识Spotify的员工，那会是多么棒的事啊！毕竟大多数公司的领导层都神秘莫测，仿佛是超脱凡尘的存在——当你在商业报道中看到他们时，总会觉得他们与现实脱节。那么，如果你能听他们畅谈一小时左右呢？这就是我的初衷。这既是招聘工具，也是为了让外界更多地了解我们的产品战略理念，更重要的是，我觉得整个过程充满乐趣。我得以采访了许多聪明且有趣的人士，包括公司内部和外部人士。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did it have the effect that you were hoping after looking back?
turns.zh: 回过头来看，你觉得它达到了你预期的效果吗？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I think it did. The podcast did well and, no, we did not give it our own promotion. I had to compete as everyone else, which also gives you a lot of empathy for the problem of like, okay, now you have a product, what about user acquisition? How do you actually get people to listen to it? So it did achieve what I wanted in the sense that we have this thing called intradays where especially in the past few years when we've hired a lot, we actually fly people to Stockholm for an onboarding session to learn about Spotify. And the leadership is on stage, talking about what they do and the departments and strategy and so forth. And it's very common that people come and tell me that, "Oh, I listened to this podcast or this and the episode and it's at least one of the key reasons why I joined or sometimes the reason why I joined." So it's anecdotal, but it may be in the many tens of people, at least, who have said it. So that seems to work.
turns.zh: 我觉得确实有效果。这期播客反响不错，不过我们并没有进行专门推广。我和其他人一样面临着同样的挑战——当你推出一个新产品后，用户获取成了首要难题。如何让人们愿意收听你的节目？从这个角度来看，这期播客达到了我的预期目标。我们每年都会举办名为"Intradays"的培训活动，过去几年招聘大量新员工时，我们会邀请他们飞往斯德哥尔摩参加入职培训，了解Spotify的运作方式。高管们会亲自上台讲解部门职责、战略规划等内容。很多参与者后来告诉我："我听了某期播客，这至少是我加入Spotify的关键原因之一，有时甚至是唯一原因。"虽然这只是个例，但据我统计，至少有几十个人都提到了这一点。看来这种宣传方式确实有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's really interesting. Just again, and this comes up a few times on the podcast, is just the power of content in all these different ways for hiring for culture building. And it sounds like the original goal was just internally build this clinic culture and strategy.
turns.zh: 真有意思。再说一次，这个话题在播客里被多次提及，那就是内容在招聘和文化建设中的强大作用。从听起来的，你们最初的目标似乎是先在内部建立起诊所的文化和战略体系。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: That was the original goal, make senior leadership more approachable and reduce the distance and then also share more of the thinking in an entertaining way rather than just through docs that people end up not reading.
turns.zh: 原本的目标是让高层领导更容易接近，缩短与员工之间的距离，同时以一种生动有趣的方式分享管理思路，而非仅仅通过人们往往不愿阅读的文档来传达信息。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. So I was listening to it, as I said, and what was really interesting is I think episode four was actually all about AI, and I think your first attempts at leveraging machine learning in AI within Spotify. And I think that's what led to Discover Weekly and a few other tools. And that was years ago. And it's interesting listening to it now where AI is, again, a huge deal. And so I'm curious very tactically on the product team what you advise product managers and product teams on how to think about AI in their product thinking and also just in their day-to-day work.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这部分。正如我之前所说，我当时一直在听那期节目，里面最有趣的部分是第四集全是关于人工智能的，还有你们最初在Spotify内部尝试利用机器学习技术做人工智能应用的经历。我记得那时候推出了"每周发现"功能和其他一些产品，而那已经是好多年前的事了。如今回头再听，发现人工智能又成了热门话题。这让我很好奇，在产品团队层面，您会给产品经理和团队成员哪些实用的建议，让他们在产品设计中更深入地思考人工智能的应用场景，以及如何将其融入日常工作中？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I can give a few examples there and I don't know that we're more sophisticated than anyone else, but we'll be doing at least the traditional machine learning for quite a long time. And I think in the podcast, I think I talked about the journey of the internet in stages. And one way to think about it is that the internet started with curation of the user curation. So you took something, some good, like people or books or music and you digitize it and you put it online, and then you ask users to curate it. And that was your Facebook, Spotify and so forth. And then after a while, the world switched from curation to recommendation, where instead of people doing that work, you had algorithms. And that was a big change that required us and others to actually rethink the entire user experience and sometimes the business model as well.
turns.zh: 我可以举几个例子，我不知道我们是否比其他人更精明，但我们至少会在很长一段时间内继续使用传统的机器学习技术。我记得在播客中，我曾谈到互联网的发展历程。可以这样理解：互联网最初是以用户内容管理为核心——你把一些优质内容（比如人力、书籍、音乐）数字化后上传到网络，然后让用户进行内容管理。这就是Facebook、Spotify等平台的模式。后来互联网从内容管理转向了推荐机制，不再由人工完成这项工作，而是由算法接管。这是一次重大变革，迫使我们和其他人不得不重新思考整个用户体验，甚至是商业模式。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And I think what we're entering now is we're going from your curation to recommendation to generation. And I suspect it will be as big of a shift that you will eventually have to rethink your products. So that's one lens. So I tend to talk to my teams about, even though it's all machine learning, I ask them to think of this as something completely different. The recommendation error was one type of machine learning. The generation error is a different type, so don't think of it as just more of the same, think of it as something actually completely new instead. And what we learned in ... Well, a few things. So if you look at this new era of large language models and the fusion models and so forth, there are two types of applications. As I said for the recommendation error, we had to rethink the user interface and the experience for recommendation first error.
turns.zh: 接下来我要讲的是，我们现在正从内容策划（curation）转向推荐（recommendation），再进而转向生成（generation）。我认为这将是一次重大变革，最终你们可能需要重新审视自己的产品。这就是第一视角。尽管这些都是机器学习的范畴，但我建议团队成员把这视为全新的领域。推荐错误属于一种类型的机器学习，而生成错误则属于另一种类型。所以别把它当作是原有技术的延续，而是要把它看作是全新的范畴。我们在……方面积累了一些经验。比如说，看看当前大语言模型和融合模型等新兴技术，应用场景可以分为两类。正如我之前提到的，在处理推荐错误时，我们首先需要重新设计推荐相关的用户界面和体验。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And so what does that mean in the generative area? No one really knows yet. As usual, there are a bunch of iterative improvements. So we use these large language models to improve our recommendations. You can have bigger vectors that can have more cultural knowledge. You can use it for safety classification on podcasts that no one has listened to yet and so forth. So there's lots of obvious improvements and we're doing those. But so far, we've only really done one real generative product in the hard definition, which is a product that couldn't have existed without generative AI, and that is the AI DJ. So that's a concept that we've been thinking about for a very long time. And the AI DJ is you press a button, a digitized person, there's a real person named X, digitized X. So he's now an AI, comes on and talks to you about music that you like and suggests music, and you can listen to it. And if you don't like it, you can just call him back and he says, "Okay, now, let's listen to something maybe from a few summers ago," or "Here's some new stuff that were trending yesterday in The Last of Us episode or something like that."
turns.zh: 那么这在生成式领域意味着什么？目前还没有人能给出确切答案。和往常一样，我们会进行一系列迭代优化。比如，我们利用大型语言模型来优化推荐算法——用户可以获得更大容量的向量数据，从而获取更多文化背景信息；还能将其应用于播客安全分类等场景。这些改进显而易见，我们也正在积极推进。但截至目前，在严格定义的生成式应用领域，我们真正推出的产品只有一个——那就是AI DJ。这款产品若没有生成式AI技术根本无法实现。AI DJ的核心玩法是：用户按下按钮后，数字化版的真人X（比如某位知名音乐人）会与你互动。系统会根据你的音乐喜好进行推荐，用户可以直接收听。若不满意推荐，用户只需重新呼叫AI DJ，它会智能调整推荐方向，比如播放几年前的热门曲目，或是推荐昨日《最后生还者》剧集中的最新潮流音乐。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So that product couldn't have existed without generative AI, both generating the voice and generating the content of what the voice says. So you can have individualized, personalized voice at the scale of half a billion people. And so we had the use case we have seen for many, many years. Sometimes people call it the radio use case. We called it the zero intent use case internally when you actually don't know what you want to listen to at all.
turns.zh: 因此，如果没有生成式人工智能，这款产品根本无法问世——无论是生成语音，还是生成语音所传达的内容。因此，你可以在五亿人的规模上实现个性化、定制化的语音体验。这种应用场景我们已经见证多年，有人将其称为广播场景。在内部，我们则将其称为"零意图场景"，即用户根本不确定自己想听什么内容时所产生的需求。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Spotify wasn't that good. Spotify was good when, at least roughly, you knew the use case of what you want to do, if it was a workout or dinner. We had lots of options for all of those. But if you really didn't know at all, it was hard to open Spotify and stare at it. And people used to say longingly that this was the one thing that radio was good at. Radio was quite bad, to be honest. I mean, it's not personalized to you at all. It's not on demand. You come in in the middle of things, it's actually terrible in many ways. But people still often say that there was something good about it. And I think that's something was the fact that you had a knob and you could just switch between contexts. It's like no, boring, boring, boring, boring, okay, this is good.
turns.zh: Spotify其实没那么好用。至少在你大致清楚自己想做什么用例时，比如锻炼或用餐时，Spotify还是挺好用的。针对这些场景，我们有很多选项。但如果你根本不知道自己想做什么，打开Spotify然后盯着它看时，就觉得很头疼。人们过去常怀念地说，收音机在这方面做得很好。但说实话，收音机其实很糟糕。它根本不针对个人定制，也没有按需播放功能。你只能在节目播放中途加入，实际上在很多方面都很糟糕。不过人们还是常说收音机有其优点。我觉得优点在于你有个旋钮，可以在不同场景间切换。比如说，不行，这个太无聊了，太无聊了，太无聊了，太无聊了，好吧，这个还不错。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And Spotify never had that mode of, I don't know what I want, but I want to cycle through things until I find something that I like. And I think with the AI DJ, that's actually the use case we managed to solve. So X comes on and says, "I'm going to suggest something to you that you can listen to." And if you like it, you can keep listening, but if you don't like it, you bring him back again and you change channel. And for one reason or another, we tried to solve that for many times for a long time, but just starting to play a random song without any context as to why you would hear this, it just never worked. So that was our first foray into a product that couldn't exist before. And I think to your question of principles around that, there are a few pretty distinct principles that we've learned.
turns.zh: 另外，Spotify从未提供过那种"我不知道自己想听什么，但我想先随机播放一遍看看有没有喜欢的"的模式。我认为通过AI DJ功能，我们成功解决了这个问题。当X出现时，它会推荐一些供你收听的音乐。如果你喜欢某首歌，就可以继续听下去；如果你不喜欢，就可以让它重新推荐。出于种种原因，我们花了很长时间反复尝试解决这个问题，但如果只是随机播放一首歌曲，却没有任何背景信息说明为什么会推荐这首歌，这种方法始终行不通。这是我们首次推出前所未有的产品。关于这个产品背后的设计原则，我认为我们总结出了一些非常明确的要点。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: One that I really like that is not my principle at all, I think it is straight from Chris Dixon, is the principle of fault-tolerant user interfaces. So I can't say how many times during the early machine learning era when we said we're moving from curation to recommendation. I saw a design sketch that was a single big play button because clearly that is the simplest user interface you can do, but if you don't understand the performance of your machine learning, you can't design for it. The quality of your machine learning, if you're going to have a single play button, needs to be literally 100% or zero prediction error, and that's never the case. So let's say that you have a one in five hits, four out of five things are done, then you need a UI that probably at least shows five things at the same time on screen. So you have a one in five of something being relevant on screen.
turns.zh: 有一条我非常推崇的原则，尽管它并非我的首创——我认为这源自克里斯·迪克森（Chris Dixon）的观点，那就是容错性用户界面的原则。在机器学习早期阶段，我曾无数次宣称我们要从人工干预转向推荐机制。当时我看到过一个设计草图，上面只有一个大大的播放按钮——显然这是最简洁的用户界面。但如果你不了解机器学习模型的性能，就无法针对其进行设计。若想采用单一播放按钮，机器学习模型的准确率必须达到100%或零预测误差，但现实情况绝非如此。假设你有五分之一的命中率，即五件事中成功四件，那么用户界面至少需要同时显示五个选项，这样屏幕上才可能有五分之一的内容是相关的。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So you need to understand the performance of your machine learning to design for it. It needs to be fault tolerant and often you need an escape hatch for the user. So you make a prediction. But if you were wrong, it needs to be super easy for the user say, "No, you're wrong, I want to go to my library or to this or to that." So we have that principle of having fault-tolerant user interface and a user interface that corresponds to the current performance of your algorithms. And I think that is going to be true for generative machine learning as well. I think a very clear example actually is Mid Journey. If you think about the early Mid Journey user interface inside the Discord channel, actually generating an image was very, very slow.
turns.zh: 因此，你需要了解机器学习模型的性能表现，才能设计出与之相匹配的界面。界面必须具备容错能力，并且通常需要为用户提供一个退出机制。例如，当模型预测错误时，用户应该能轻松纠正错误，例如"不，你错了，我想去我的图书馆，或者去别的地方"。基于此，我们秉持的原则是，用户界面要具备容错能力，并且要与算法当前的性能表现相适应。我认为这一原则同样适用于生成式机器学习领域。一个非常典型的例子就是Mid Journey。如果你回想起Discord频道内早期Mid Journey的用户界面，会发现生成图像的速度极其缓慢。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: It took a long time to generate high-quality image and they could have built the silver button thing where you put in a prompt, you wait for minutes, you get an image, and I think one out of four times, it's going to be bad. So you would've been disappointed three out of four times and it's a minute each, so like four minutes later, you'd be, "This is a shitty product." What they did was they generated four simultaneous low-res images very quickly and you could say, "So apparently, their performance was probably one in four, that's why they showed four and not six." And so one in four was usually pretty good. You click that one and either continue to iterate or scale it up. So that's also an example of, I think, people understanding where the performance of generative AI was when they built the UI. So that's something that I would be inspired by.
turns.zh: 生成高质量图像需要很长时间。他们本可以设计一个银色按钮界面——用户输入提示语后，等待几分钟就能获得图像。但我觉得四次尝试中大概有三次结果不理想。这样一来，用户每四次尝试就要花费四分钟时间，最终难免会感到失望，忍不住抱怨"这产品太烂了"。他们的解决方案是同时快速生成四张低分辨率图像，这样用户就能明白："显然他们的生成模型准确率只有四分之一，所以才展示了四张而不是六张。"而这四张中的某一张通常还算不错。用户点击满意的图像后，可以继续迭代优化或放大尺寸。这也让我深受启发——我认为这体现了开发者在设计用户界面时，充分预估了生成式AI的实际性能上限。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And for the AI DJ specifically, another principle is to try to avoid this urge of just wanting to show off the technology and then have this voice that talk and talk and talk and talk. You have to remember that people came there for the music. So the principle for the AI DJ coming from the team, by the way, this was a bottoms-up product actually, it required a lot of support. We actually acquired big companies and so forth to be able to build it. But the idea had been built by teams bottom up. So the principle there was literally to do as little as possible and get out of the way. And I think that was really helpful. It's not telling you what the weather is and what happened in the news and going on and on and on about this band. It is trying to get you to the music and I think that's why it's working because it is working very well for us.
turns.zh: 特别是对于AI DJ而言，另一个原则是尽可能避免那种只想炫技、然后让语音系统不停讲个不停的冲动。请记住，人们来这里是为了听音乐。所以，顺便说一句，AI DJ这个产品是自下而上开发的，确实需要大量支持。我们还收购了大公司等资源来完成开发，但最初的创意完全源自团队内部。当时的核心理念就是尽量减少干预，让用户专注于音乐体验。我认为这非常有效。它不会跟你讲天气预报、新闻头条，也不会没完没了地夸赞某支乐队。它专注于引导你直达音乐核心，这也是它能成功的关键——至少对我们而言效果显著。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this distinction between recommendation and generation. And this begs the question of, there's this trend that I imagine you're seeing of people autogenerating music using artists catalog. There's this Drake and The Weeknd thing that came out a week or two ago. Where do you think this ends up going and how do you think artists adjust to this world where music can just be autogenerated? This play button is all of it is generated versus just like the DJ in between the songs.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏推荐与生成音乐之间的这种区分。这也引发了一个问题——我相信你也注意到了，人们正热衷于利用艺术家目录自动生成音乐。前不久，Drake和The Weeknd合作的作品引发了热议。你认为这种趋势会如何发展？艺术家该如何适应这个音乐可以被自动生成的时代？这个播放按钮所播放的音乐，全都是自动生成的，而非DJ在歌曲间切换的传统方式。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: First, big caveat, this is just super early. No one knows anything about how this is going to play out or the legal landscape and so forth, but I think it's going to have a lot of impact. And I think if we talk about two things, one is what it could do for music, the other is the right situation, and if rights-holders are getting compensated and so forth. So we talk about the first thing in isolation. I think an interesting example is right about when I grew up, Avicii came along. And it's interesting to think about because Avicii was not really considered by the existing music industry as a real artist because he couldn't really play an instrument and he couldn't sing, and he was just sitting with this computer in this DAW, digital audio workstation. And so it wasn't really considered real music. And I think now all of us consider it very real music and that he had tremendous real musical talent.
turns.zh: 首先，要说明一点，目前这一切都还处于早期阶段。没人能预料后续的发展态势、法律环境等诸多变数，但我认为这项技术将产生深远影响。若要探讨其影响，关键在于两点：其一，它能为音乐产业带来哪些机遇；其二，相关权利方能否获得合理补偿并确保利益分配。先就前者展开讨论。一个耐人寻味的例子发生在我成长的那个时代——当艾维奇（Avicii）横空出世之际。回首往事会发现，当时传统音乐行业并不认可他为真正的艺术家，因为他既不会演奏乐器，也不具备专业歌唱技巧，仅是坐在DAW（数字音频工作站）前进行创作。这种音乐形式当时被视为非主流产物。但如今，我们都认可他是货真价实的音乐人，且他展现出了卓越的音乐才华。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So I think right now, we're probably in the face where people say this isn't real music and it's somehow fake. I think the way to think about these diffusion models if and when they get good enough at generating music is probably the same like an instrument. It's just a much more powerful instrument and we'll probably see a new type of creator that wasn't proficient at any instrument and they couldn't assemble a full orchestra and do the thing that they had in their head and they can now generate very new things. I also think, by the way, that there is this distinction between AI music and real music that doesn't exist. For sure, very talented real musicians are using AI to get better and to help create new ideas. So that distinction doesn't really exist. It's all going to be AI. The question is what percentage, which makes the problem harder because you can't talk about if it should exist or not.
turns.zh: 因此，我认为当下人们可能会认为这种音乐不算"真正的音乐"，认为它存在某种虚假感。但当这些生成模型在音乐创作方面足够出色时，我们或许可以将其视为另一种乐器。只不过这是一款功能更为强大的乐器。我们很可能会看到一类新型的创作者——那些原本不精通任何乐器、无法组建完整管弦乐队、也无法实现脑海中构想的音乐创作的人，如今却能生成全新的音乐作品。顺便说一句，我认为所谓"AI音乐"与"真正音乐"之间的界限其实并不存在。当然，许多才华横溢的真人音乐家正在借助AI技术提升创作水平、激发灵感。所以这种界限根本不存在。未来一切都将由AI主导。关键问题在于，AI的贡献比例究竟有多大？而这个比例的确定难度极大，因为我们无法断言它是否应该存在。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: You have to talk about what percentage should exist and who gets to use it or not. But I think the way to think about it is probably as an instrument and that could help create a huge amount of art. And I think this is not news to you who probably use these things a lot, but I think if you don't use these generative models, there is the perception that you tell it to create a hit and you will get that. That's not how it works. Actually, what these models do is because they've been listening to a lot of music, they are very good at doing something that sounds very similar to what already exists. Actually being original is very hard. And from one point of view, as it now gets easier to create more generic music, it will actually be more difficult than ever to be truly unique.
turns.zh: 你们得探讨一下应该保留多大比例的素材，以及谁能使用、谁不能使用。但我觉得看待这件事的角度或许可以把它视为一种创作工具，它能助力创作出大量艺术作品。我想对于经常使用这些工具的你们来说，这应该不算新闻。但我认为，如果不使用生成式模型，人们可能会认为只要告诉它创作一首热门歌曲就能成功。但事实并非如此。实际上，生成式模型之所以能创作出与已有作品极为相似的作品，是因为它们听过大量音乐，擅长模仿已有的风格。真正原创其实非常难。从某种角度看，随着生成更具普适性的音乐变得更加容易，想要真正实现独特性反而会比以往更加困难。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So I still think there would be tremendous skill in creating something truly unique. And my hope would be that what happened with the DAW and that technology jump was you got a whole new genre like EDM that you couldn't really produce it with an orchestra or live. And maybe we'll see completely new music styles with these technologies. I think that would be very exciting. So that's on the positive side, but then you have the rights issue, which I have a lot of empathy for. And Spotify specifically has seen this before. So we had a different technology shift like this, which was the technology shift to online downloads of music and piracy and peer to peer. So first, it was a big technology shift in peer to peer and it was exciting for consumers. More consumers started listening to more music than ever. And I think that's where we are now with generative AI.
turns.zh: 因此，我仍然认为创造出真正独一无二的东西需要极高的技艺。我希望看到DAW（数字音频工作站）带来的技术飞跃能催生出全新的音乐类型，比如电子舞曲（EDM）——这种音乐用传统乐队或现场演出根本无法创作。或许借助这些新技术，我们还能见证全新的音乐风格诞生。我觉得这会非常令人兴奋。这是积极的一面，但随之而来的版权问题也值得关注。对此我深表同情，Spotify就曾亲身经历过类似的挑战。比如，当年音乐从实体载体向在线下载转变时，盗版和P2P（点对点）传输问题引发了行业动荡。最初，P2P技术带来了激动人心的创新，吸引了更多听众，音乐消费量空前增长。如今，生成式AI技术同样引发了行业巨变，值得我们密切关注。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: There's a new technology, but it also required a new business model before creators and industry could actually participate and benefit from this. And that's, obviously, self-serving to say because we were a big part of innovating that business model. But I still think that's what's necessary and I hope that that's what I and we could be part of. So I think we've seen the first part, the technology shift, and there will probably be a lot of discussion and chaos here which have a lot of empathy for, but I think we haven't seen the second part yet. What is a model where this could be a benefit? What actually happened after piracy is that the music industry got bigger than ever, not just as big but bigger than ever. And I think that could happen with this technology as well. But we're right in the beginning.
turns.zh: 有一项新技术，但在创作者和行业真正参与并从中获益之前，还需要一个全新的商业模式。说这话显然是自利的，因为我们在创新这种商业模式方面发挥了重要作用。但我仍然认为这是必要的，希望我和我们团队能参与其中。所以我们已经见证了第一阶段——技术变革，接下来很可能还会有诸多讨论和混乱。对此我深表同情，但我认为第二阶段尚未到来。一个能带来实质性收益的商业模式应该是什么样的？在打击盗版之后，音乐行业不仅规模空前扩大，而且比以往任何时候都更繁荣。我相信这项技术也将带来类似的机遇。但我们目前还处在起步阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So along the same lines, something else you teach is this idea of all truly great products have to pull some magic trick. This comes up in your podcast a lot and I think you mentioned this other places, and thinking about all the stuff you're talking about here, it feels like, in a sense, everything's going to feel like magic because AI's baked into it.
turns.zh: 同理，你所传授的另一个理念是，所有真正伟大的产品都必须能上演某种"魔术般的奇迹"。这在你的播客中多次被提及，我想你也在其他场合谈及过这个观点。综合你在这里提到的所有内容，似乎一切都将如同魔术般令人惊叹，因为人工智能已深度融入其中。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I think when we did the AI DJ, we did a small version of that. When people first listened to it, we could see that reaction in use of testing when they've wondered ... So the magic trick there was that how could they record this person saying so many different things because it's talking about my music. So the magic trick was, obviously, didn't record a person saying, it's generated, and that magic trick wears off. You hear it all the time now and so forth, but it was one of those magic tricks. So I still think that concept is important and it seems to correlate with products going viral and taking off.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们做AI DJ那次，就是把这个概念小规模化了。刚开始人们听的时候，我们能从他们的反应中看出测试效果——他们会疑惑……所以这里的魔术在于，如何让一个人说出这么多不同的内容，因为这些内容都是关于我的音乐的。所以魔术的关键显然不是录制真人发言，而是通过生成技术实现的。但这种魔术效果终究会消失。如今大家常听到类似的案例，但这就是其中一个经典魔术。我仍然认为这个概念很重要，它似乎与产品迅速走红、引发病毒式传播有着密切关联。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And I think it was the same using something like Dall-E or Stable Diffusion or Mid Journey the first time. It completely seemed like a magic trick. And, obviously, there is no magic, it's just data and statistics. But I think getting to that point and iterating a product to the point where it feels like magic the first time is very helpful. And it's often a question of just getting the performance to a certain level, scoping down, removing things. There's a lot of fine-tuning, I think, that makes you cross that line from it's cool and impressive but not magic to it feels like magic. I don't understand how this could be done.
turns.zh: 还有，我觉得第一次使用Dall-E、Stable Diffusion或Mid Journey之类的工具时，感觉就跟魔术一样。显然这背后没有魔法，只是数据和统计的运作。但我认为能达到那种效果，并将产品迭代到第一次使用就让人感觉神奇的境界，确实非常有帮助。这往往需要把性能提升到一定水平，再进行精简、去除冗余。关键在于微调，让产品从"很酷、令人惊叹但不神奇"，跨越到"感觉充满魔力"的境界。我还是不明白这怎么做到的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it reminds me of the launch of GBT which ended up being the biggest, most fastest growing product in history, and it's like the epitome of a magic trick. It feels like actual magic.
turns.zh: 是啊，这让我想起GBT的发布——它最终成为史上规模最大、增长最快的产品，简直就是魔术般的杰作。那种感觉就好像见证了真正的魔术表演。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Absolutely, absolutely. And to most people, it is still very ... Actually to a lot of ascent, even to researchers, it's a little bit magical. No one really understands fully. So I guess there's maybe some magic left in the world.
turns.zh: 没错，确实如此。对大多数人而言，这仍然非常……实际上，对于许多探索者，甚至是研究人员来说，这都带有几分神秘色彩。没人能完全参透其奥秘。所以我想，或许这世间仍残存着些许魔力吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. And I think a lot of people are worried about not understanding what's going on there. Shifting to the way you all build product at Spotify. So Spotify is famous for popularizing this idea of squads and tribes. And correct me if I'm wrong, but you guys have moved away from that approach.
turns.zh: 完全正确。我觉得很多人都担心不了解那里正在发生什么。接下来谈谈你们在Spotify的产品开发方式。Spotify以推广"小团队"和"部落"模式而闻名。请纠正我一下，如果我理解有误的话，但你们现在已经不再沿用这种方法了。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Yeah, that's right.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So I'd love to understand just why you shifted and what you learned from that approach to building product, and then just like how do you organize the teams now? What do you do now?
turns.zh: 好的。所以我很想了解一下你为什么会做出调整，从那次产品开发策略中吸取了哪些教训。然后再说说你现在是如何组织团队的？现在都做些什么？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: This was something that we focused a lot on early and it turned out to be smart of us to name these things into squads and chapters and so forth. It wasn't really ... Well, maybe it was deliberately branding, but it wasn't for purposes of branding that we made it up. We made it up because we thought it was a good structure to use and we needed names for things and this was the early internet eras you were allowed to make things up. And so it was very good for where we were at the time and it certainly helped us in recruiting. It's become a little bit of a cost to us because people still think that we organize that way and it's not a very efficient way of being organized at this scale or maybe even if you started over right now because we've learned more.
turns.zh: 这是我们早期非常重视的一件事。结果证明，把这些组织划分成小组、章节等，是个明智之举。这其实并非……好吧，或许这确实是刻意打造品牌形象，但我们这么做并非为了品牌推广。我们之所以这样做，是因为我们认为这是一种有效的组织架构，而且当时互联网尚处早期阶段，人们可以自由发挥创意。因此，这种架构在当时的环境下非常适用，也确实帮助我们招募了不少人才。但如今这已成为一种隐性成本，因为外界至今仍误以为我们沿用着这种组织模式。但这种组织方式在当今这个规模下效率极低——即便现在重新规划，也未必能改善现状，毕竟我们已经积累了更多经验。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: But I think the big difference is the idea with the squad specifically was twofold. They were supposed to be small and full stack. So squad should be about seven people and it should have front and backend, mobile, QA, agile coaches and so forth, and it should be very autonomous was the idea. And that's really what we shifted. So, first of all, as you grow the company, scaling in increments of seven engineers just creates a ton of overhead. So, obviously, our teams now tend to be much bigger, maybe two, three times that at least per manager to maybe have 14 or something instead of seven and just less overhead roles. So that's one. It looks more traditional as you learn more and is reasonable as you scale. The second big thing I think we struggle with was back then when I joined, the average age at Spotify was ... I mean, I was the oldest and this was 14 years ago. So I think the average age was probably under 30 or something and it wasn't most tech companies.
turns.zh:
但我认为最大的区别在于，关于小组的理念有两个核心要点。首先，小组应该规模小且功能齐全。理想的团队规模约为7人，涵盖前端、后端、移动端、QA、敏捷教练等角色，并且要具备高度自治能力。这正是我们所做出的调整。  

首先，随着公司规模的扩大，按7名工程师为一组进行扩容会产生大量管理冗余。显然，如今我们的团队规模要大得多——每个经理管理的团队规模至少是原来的两到三倍，可能达到14人左右，同时减少了重复的管理岗位。这是第一点。在团队规模扩大的过程中，更传统的组织架构更易于管理，也更符合规模化发展的逻辑。  

第二个难点是，我加入Spotify时，公司的平均年龄……我是当时最年长的，那是在14年前。所以我猜当时公司的平均年龄可能不到30岁，而这在大多数科技公司中并不常见。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And so we had coming from Sweden, which is a different culture than the US, and I love a lot of things about Swedish culture and I think we managed to keep the best parts, but Sweden is a very bottoms-up autonomous culture. There's this famous drawing on how you make decisions in Sweden. In the US, I think it's just a hierarchy. In Sweden, it's a circle. It's in a circle, no one is in the middle, there is no leader and so forth.
turns.zh: 因此，我们来自瑞典，这里与美国有着截然不同的文化。我非常喜欢瑞典文化的诸多方面，我认为我们成功保留了其精华所在。不过，瑞典是一种自下而上的自主文化。有一幅著名的漫画，生动诠释了瑞典人的决策方式。在美国，我认为决策权往往集中在 hierarchy（等级制度）中；而在瑞典，决策则呈现出 circle（循环）的形态。决策过程是环形的，没有任何人处于核心地位，也没有所谓的领导者等特定角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting.
turns.zh: 真有意思。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So I think by culture, we're very inspired by this super autonomous thing. And I think the idea with autonomy is very reasonable and the right one, which is we work and we are hiring the smartest people we can find and we pay high salaries for that. So if you're hiring smart people, one way to think about it is you're renting brain power.
turns.zh: 因此，我认为从文化层面来讲，我们深受这种高度自主性事物的启发。我认为自主性这一理念是十分合理且正确的——我们努力工作，尽可能聘请最优秀的人才，并为此支付高额薪酬。所以当你招募人才时，可以把这看作是在租用他们的智力资源。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So if you're renting all of this expensive brain power and then you give them no room to think for themselves, that doesn't sound smart, then you should actually hire less smart people and keep your costs down or something. So I think you have to give a bunch of autonomy to actually maximize the value of the investment you're making. So that's very reasonable that you would give a lot of space for people to use as much of their talent and capacity as possible. But the problem with that is if you put autonomy very far towards the leaves of the organization, and also if you combine that with having a very junior organization, which we did back then, there's a fair chance that you're just going to produce heat. You're going to have a hundred squads with a hundred strategies running in a hundred directions. And Spotify has been there in that camp.
turns.zh: 因此，如果你租用了所有这些高昂的智力资源，却不给他们自主思考的空间，这显然不明智。那么你或许应该雇佣能力稍弱的人员，以降低成本。我的观点是，要想充分发挥投资价值，就必须赋予员工充分的自主权。让员工最大限度地发挥自身才能和潜力，这无疑是明智之举。但问题在于，如果将自主权下放至组织的末端，再加上组织架构过于扁平化（就像我们当时所做的那样），很有可能导致内部资源浪费。届时，数百个团队会各自制定数百种战略，各自为政。Spotify就曾深陷过这样的困境。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I mean, we managed to get somewhere, for sure, in spite of this, but I'd struggle to say we were efficient in doing that. So we've done a few things. The team structure is more traditional, larger teams, less overhead. And we've been specifically working with where in the org do we put the autonomy because the extremes are at the leaves and we were there. The other extreme may be at the top, let's say maybe some Twitter, there's one person. Both have problems. If you have it at the leaves, you're going to produce a lot of heat. If you have it at the top, you need someone with a lot of capacity and Elon has a lot of capacity, but you are, by definition, going to bottleneck. All decisions have to go through there. And Daniel, it's not his personality that he even wants to make all the decisions.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，尽管如此，我们确实取得了一些成果，但很难说我们做事高效。我们采取了一些措施。团队结构更传统，团队规模更大，管理成本更低。我们一直在研究在组织中如何赋予自主权，因为极端情况下，一端是权力下放到基层员工，我们曾处于这种境地；另一端则可能是权力高度集中于高层，比如推特公司，整个公司可能就由一个人负责。两种极端情况都有问题。如果权力下放到基层，容易引发内部混乱；如果权力高度集中于高层，虽然能提高决策效率，但注定会形成决策瓶颈，所有重大决策都必须经过高层审批。丹尼尔（Daniel）并非天生就想独自包办所有决策——这跟他的性格无关。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: He wants to maximize throughput rather than to bottleneck the throughput. So the question is, if it's not at the top and not at the very bottom, where do you put it? And what we've found, which I don't think is very contrarian at all, I think this is the case in most companies, is around the VP level. So if you have Daniel, then you have the C level, myself and others, then you have the VP level, that is a good mix of instead of having one person in the company think, so only Daniel then and the rest just do, you have on the VP level in the company this many tens to maybe hundreds of people that have a lot of autonomy to think. So you get a good amount of freedom of thought and people thinking in different directions, but it's not like 8,000 people. And these people on the VP level are both quite a lot of them, but they're also usually quite senior. They have a lot of pattern recognition.
turns.zh: 他希望最大化生产效率，而不是造成生产瓶颈。所以问题在于，如果既不是处于最高层，也不是处于最低层，那该把他们放在哪里呢？我们发现的一个现象——我认为这并不算反常规——在大多数公司里都是如此，那就是把他们安排在副总裁级别。假设公司里有丹尼尔（Daniel）这样的高管，那么C级高管、我自己以及其他人则属于VP级别。这种结构能形成良好的平衡——既不让公司里某个人独自思考决策（比如只有丹尼尔说了算，其他人只能服从），也让VP级别的员工拥有大量自主思考的空间。因此，公司能汇聚大量独立思考的智慧，形成多元的思路碰撞，但又不会让8000人同时参与其中。VP级别的员工数量众多，而且通常资历深厚，拥有丰富的经验和敏锐的洞察力。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So I think that solves for, it's a good ... If you think of it as an optimization problem, it's a good optimization space. So the autonomy level in Spotify now tends to be quite high at the VP level and then lower around those levels.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得这就解决了问题，这是一个不错的……如果你把它看作一个优化问题，那这是一个很好的优化空间。现在Spotify的自主权水平在VP级别通常相当高，而在更低级别则有所降低。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And when you say autonomy, what does that actually mean? Is it the VP of, say, the podcasting product has a lot of say over what happens and there's not a ton of ... I don't know how involved are people above? And I know Maya's the VP of product, I believe, for the podcast product.
turns.zh: 还有，当你提到“自主权”时，具体指的是什么？比如说，播客产品部门的副总裁是否对业务决策有很大话语权？上级管理层又有多少参与度呢？据我所知，玛雅应该就是播客产品线的副总裁。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Who I think is going to come on the podcast someday. What does that mean in terms of Tommy for her, what practically?
turns.zh: 谁是我认为未来某天会参加播客节目的嘉宾。就她而言，这对汤米意味着什么？具体来说会有怎样的合作呢？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So it means that I would ask Maya to define a strategy for what we do in podcasting, how are we going to be different, why would a podcaster want to be here? Whereas another company, I will make that strategy or another company, Daniel would make that strategy. Same with ... The AI DJ, for example, came from our personalization team. And so that was a bet that they made. So they have autonomy to make those kinds of bets and define strategies. Same with the user interface, we have an experienced team, can talk about the org structure later, but I put a lot of autonomy on the VP of experience to define and suggest what it is that we want to do. And in other companies, I would define all of that myself, for example.
turns.zh: 也就是说，我会让玛雅为我们的播客业务制定战略——我们要如何与众不同？为什么播客主会愿意加入我们？而在其他公司，可能是由我来制定这项战略，或者由丹尼尔来负责。同样，比如人工智能DJ项目，就源自我们的个性化团队。这是他们做出的一个决策。他们有自主权来做这样的决策并制定战略。用户界面方面，我们也有一个经验丰富的团队。稍后再详细讲组织架构，但我赋予了体验副总裁很大的自主权，让他来定义和提出我们想要做的事情。而在其他公司，这些决策可能都由我自己来制定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just going even a little bit further here, I know you have just strong opinions on the way to organize teams and how the organization helps you optimize for specific things. What are your just thoughts along those lines and what have you learned about how the impact of organization and what you're optimizing for?
turns.zh: 稍微深入一点说，我知道你对团队组织方式以及组织如何帮助优化特定目标有着强烈的见解。关于这些方面，你有什么独到见解？你又对组织的影响以及所优化目标的实际效果有何深刻体会？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Yeah. So I talk about an idealized spectrum or maybe not idealized but exaggerated spectrum. Nothing is really true, but you create extremes to make a point. So on one spectrum, you have something like Amazon, which is known for two-pizza teams, no dependencies. You try to minimize dependencies so you can run in parallel. Teams compete with each other even on the same project and so forth. But they have direct access to the user.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我所谈论的是一个理想化的光谱——或者说不算理想化，但也夸大了某些方面。没有什么是绝对正确的，但你需要通过极端的例子来阐明观点。比如亚马逊这样的公司，以"两个比萨团队"、"零依赖"为特点，尽可能减少团队之间的依赖关系，以便并行开展工作。即便是在同一个项目中，团队之间也会相互竞争。最重要的是，他们能直接接触到用户。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And so the benefit here is if you have an idea, the time to get the user is very low and it has worked for them. It's produced Kindle, it produced Alexa, it's produced a lot of very novel things. There are a few interesting downsides here. One downside that I'm extremely impressed with Jeff Bezos' foreseeing is if you have teams that compete with each other, the incentives are to hide your results, hide your code. And that should make for an organization that gets no platform leverage because no one's corporating. And I think either he had that insight or because he saw this, he had to do this, but he's well known for pushing extremely hard on hard APIs. If you don't create hard APIs to your technology, you're out. And if you think about it, it has to be that way because otherwise no one would do it.
turns.zh: 因此，这里的好处在于，如果你有了一个想法，那么获取用户的时间成本会非常低，而且这种模式已经为亚马逊带来了成功案例。比如Kindle、Alexa等创新产品，亚马逊在众多领域都创造了许多开创性的成果。不过这种模式也存在一些值得关注的弊端。其中一个让我对杰夫·贝索斯的远见卓识印象深刻的弊端是，当团队之间存在竞争关系时，团队成员往往会倾向于隐藏自己的成果和代码。这会导致整个组织无法充分利用平台优势，因为大家都各自为战。我认为贝索斯之所以如此强调严格的API标准，要么是因为他预见到了这个问题，或者是因为他亲眼目睹了其危害。亚马逊素来以在API标准上极其严苛著称——如果你不为自己的技术制定严格的API标准，你就注定会被淘汰。仔细想想，这也是必然的选择，否则谁会愿意遵守这些规则呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And a hard API is essentially everyone knows how to use this API and connect to this team to interface with.
turns.zh: 一个硬性API实质上就是每个人都知道如何使用这个API，并与这个团队对接以实现交互。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Exactly. You have to expose your technology to others. You have to maintain those APIs and they have to be very structured because otherwise the whole thing would collapse as everyone's supposed to compete because there are no incentives. You have to centrally force that. And interestingly, even though theoretically then they're the worst position to have a structured platform, I think, because they forced it so hard, they were the ones who did Amazon Web Services because they had such hard defined APIs because of this rule that it was easier for them to turn it inside out and expose it the rest of the world. Whereas if you look at someone like Google, I think they struggled more with externalizing their APIs maybe because it is so friendly and soft. So they didn't need as hard APIs on the inside because there was no competition. People could just go into each other's code.
turns.zh: 没错。你必须向他人开放你的技术。必须维护这些API，并且它们必须高度结构化，否则整个系统就会崩溃，因为所有人都必须参与竞争，却没有任何激励机制。这就需要中央强制推行这种规范。值得注意的是，尽管从理论上讲，亚马逊作为API结构化平台的典型例子，本应处于最不利的地位，但由于他们严格执行了这一规则，反而成为首批推出Amazon Web Services（AWS）的企业。正是因为API定义严格，AWS才能轻松实现内外开放。相反，拿谷歌来说，他们在开放API方面遇到的阻力更大——或许是因为谷歌的开发环境过于友好，内部API不需要过于严格的规范，因为没有竞争压力，开发者可以随意访问彼此的代码。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So it's interesting anecdote around it, but the main point is you're faster there, but it's going to be hard to corporate. And so you will see something like maybe exaggerating a bit. Sometimes you'll see multiple search boxes on the same page from different teams. And this has been true in Spotify, by the way, as well. You've seen multiple toasters on the Now Playing view coming up from different teams because they're working. When we were in the autonomous mode, everyone running. And then ... So you get the benefit of speed, but you get the drawback of shipping your org chart and shipping complexity to the end user. But clearly, that's been the right choice for Amazon because they're a trillion-dollar company. But then on the other spectrum, you have something like Apple who's also a trillion-dollar company. So clearly, both models work, where you would never see two search boxes from the same team popping up on an iPhone. That is centrally organized by something that is close to single individual.
turns.zh: 关于这件事有个有趣的趣闻，但关键点在于，尽管开发速度更快，但要想实现协作却很困难。比如，你可能会看到一些夸大其词的做法。有些页面上会出现来自不同团队的多个搜索框。顺便说一句，Spotify也曾出现过这种情况——在播放界面上，多个来自不同团队的Toaster组件会同时弹出，因为各团队都在忙于开发。当我们处于自主模式时，所有团队都在各自忙碌。而后……虽然能享受到开发速度带来的好处，但最终却把组织架构和复杂性暴露给了用户。不过显然，亚马逊选择了这种模式，毕竟它是一家市值万亿美元的巨头。但另一方面，苹果作为同样市值万亿美元的公司，却走的是另一条路线——在iPhone上，绝不会出现同一团队开发的两个搜索框同时弹出的情况。这背后离不开近乎单人化的集中管理模式。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So they are instead in what is probably the world's biggest largest functional org, they're doing as much. If you think about what goes into the Apple, I mean, they certainly do everything we do. They have music service, podcast service, audiobooks, and they have a billion other services. So it's not like they have an easier problem. And yet they build something that feels more like it was built by a single developer for a single user. So they centralize and they have this bottlenecking function that everything has to go through and be decided how it fits with everything else. And so that has the benefit of the user experience being simpler and not shipping the org chart and increasing complexity. But it also has the drawback of speed without having facts on it. I've heard people working at Apple have said, "Yeah, it took seven years to get that thing to market," because you just had to wait in the pipeline.
turns.zh: 因此，他们实际上身处可能是全球规模最大的功能性组织中，而且业务开展得如火如荼。若仔细审视苹果公司的业务版图——音乐服务、播客服务、有声书服务以及其他数十项服务——就会发现，他们所做的一切与我们并无二致。换句话说，他们的挑战与我们并无本质区别。然而，苹果却能打造出给人感觉仿佛由单个开发者为单个用户量身打造的体验。他们的核心策略是将资源高度集中化，通过一套严密的管控机制，确保所有创新成果都能与现有体系无缝衔合。这种模式固然能简化用户体验，避免组织结构复杂化，但同时也存在效率受限的弊端——由于缺乏实时反馈机制，产品研发进程往往会被无限期拖延。据我所知，苹果内部有员工曾坦言："那款产品花了七年时间才推向市场"，因为每个创新点都必须在层层审批中历经漫长等待。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So you have these extremes. And I think the most interesting example, I think, to think about is when you double click the power button on an iPhone, the Apple Pay comes up. That decision, how did that happen? You can imagine that all the services team would like to pop up when you double click that button. And so someone had to decide, should music come up, should payments come up, should something else come up? And so they have a different structure there. And on that spectrum of centralized versus decentralized, because of our strategy, which is we're a single application, trying to add or not trying to, we have added multiple types of content with actually very different business models on the backend, rev shares and royalties and book deals and so forth into single user experience. That is our strategy. We think the user experience in keeping that simple is the most important thing.
turns.zh: 因此，我们会看到两种极端情况。我认为最有趣的例子是，当你双击iPhone的电源按钮时，Apple Pay会弹出。那么这个设计是如何实现的呢？你可以想象，所有服务团队都希望在你双击电源按钮时弹出各自的界面。但最终必须有人做出决定：是让音乐界面出现，还是支付界面，或者其他内容？因此，他们采用了不同的架构设计。在中心化与去中心化这两个维度上，由于我们的策略是打造单一应用，我们既不刻意添加新功能，也不刻意去除旧功能。我们将背后的不同商业模式（如版税分成、书籍交易等）整合到统一的用户体验中。这就是我们的策略。我们认为保持用户体验的简洁性是最为重要的。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So we've chosen more of the centralized model, where these different vertical businesses, if you think about it, the music business, podcast, audiobooks business, they have it to go through a single recommendation organization because that's another problem. Which one do you recommend to which user? Should be a book or podcast or music? And how do you weigh them against each other? And also the user interface could easily get incredibly complicated if everyone built their own UI. The music team built their UI and then someone added features on top. So that's how we chose to optimize. But it is based on our strategy and I think both models work.
turns.zh: 因此，我们选择了更偏向于集中式模式。在这种模式下，各类垂直业务（比如音乐业务、播客业务、有声书业务）都需要通过一个统一的推荐机制来实现协同，因为这又引出了另一个问题——该向哪个用户推荐哪种内容？是书籍、播客还是音乐？如何在它们之间进行权衡？如果每个团队都各自开发用户界面（UI），情况会变得极其复杂。音乐团队开发了自己的UI，随后其他团队又在此基础上添加了新功能。这就是我们选择优化模式的初衷。不过，这种设计思路是基于我们的整体策略制定的，而且我认为两种模式各有其优点。

Learn more at eco.com/lenny, that's E-C-O.com/lenny.
