turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting these two examples you gave, Apple and Amazon, they're two of the biggest companies in the world and they're like at the extremes of these two into the spectrum. And it's interesting, most companies are somewhere in the middle. I wonder if there's just a benefit to being in an extreme and that ends up being really important.
turns.zh: 你提到的两个例子——苹果和亚马逊——确实很有意思。它们是全球最大的两家公司，分别处于这个光谱的两个极端。值得注意的是，大多数公司都处于两者之间的某个位置。我在想，是否处于极端状态反而会带来某种优势，最终成为至关重要的竞争力呢？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I think so. In almost all industries, you have this smiling curve concept, where you want to be at the extremes on the smiling curve, and that's where big business opportunities are but not in the middle. So it's probably true in terms of organizational models as well.
turns.zh: 我觉得是这样的。在几乎所有行业中，都存在着"微笑曲线"这个概念——你希望自己的位置处于微笑曲线的两端，因为那里蕴藏着巨大的商业机遇，而中间位置则并非如此。因此，在组织模式方面，这一观点也很有道理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of extremes, I want to talk a bit about taking big bets. So you guys had this big launch event recently where you basically redesigned the whole primary feed of Spotify to make it feel more like where apps are going, like TikTok reels feel of just stream, and you start hearing videos and music starts playing and some people loved it, some people did not. And I'm curious as a product leader, how you think about thinking long term and dealing with people that are just like, "What the hell's ... I hate change, stop changing things." How do you think about that? Who do you listen to? Who do you ignore? How do you know to stay the course? How do you approach that?
turns.zh: 说到极端情况，我想谈谈冒大风险的问题。你们最近举办了一场盛大的发布活动，彻底重构了Spotify的主流信息流界面，让它更符合当下应用的发展趋势——比如TikTok的Reels功能，用户只需点击播放就能直接观看视频和音乐。有些人对此赞不绝口，有些人则表示反感。我很好奇，作为产品负责人，你们如何看待长远规划，以及如何应对那些"这到底怎么回事……我讨厌变化，别再改了"之类抱怨的用户？你们如何权衡取舍？该听取谁的意见？又该忽视谁的反对？如何确定前进的方向？该如何处理这种情况？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Yeah, you're being very kind. There was a lot of negative feedback on Twitter on some of that. So let me actually dig into some detail because I think for product people listening to this, this is an interesting lesson that I think few companies talk about because you want talk about everything that went exactly as you thought they would and you don't want to talk about the things that didn't go exactly as you thought they would.
turns.zh: 是啊，你真是太客气了。推特上对此事有很多负面反馈。所以让我深入探讨一些细节吧，我觉得对于听众中的产品从业者来说，这是一个很有启发的教训。恐怕很少有公司会主动谈论这些问题，因为大家总想把事情描述得尽善尽美，却不愿提及那些未能如愿的部分。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So I'll go through what we are trying to achieve and what we learned. So Spotify is mainly a background application, and for a long time, we've been considered very good at background music and podcast recommendation. When the phone is in your pocket and you're listening to an EDM playlist or pop playlist or something, we're really good at inserting another EDM track there or another pop track there or something like that in the background.
turns.zh: 接下来，我会讲讲我们试图达成的目标以及我们学到了什么。Spotify主要是一款后台应用程序，很长一段时间以来，我们在背景音乐和播客推荐方面一直表现出色。当手机放在口袋里，而你正在听电子舞曲播放列表、流行歌曲播放列表之类的内容时，我们非常擅长在后台插入另一首电子舞曲或流行歌曲等内容。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: What we hear from users again and again, though, is that they say that they get trapped in a taste bubble. So I love my Spotify, I love this, but I'm a little bit bored with EDM now and Spotify's not suggesting something completely new. And if you think about that problem, it may sound similar to the recommendation problem, it's just another recommendation problem, but it's actually fundamentally different because when you're recommending another EDM track inside the EDM playlist, you have a lot of signal from that user that they like EDM. But if you're going to recommend a completely new genre, by definition, you have no idea. Because if you had an idea, it wasn't new to them. So you can't know anything. So back to hit rate, your hit rate is going to be incredibly low when you suggest something completely new to the user.
turns.zh: 然而，我们反复从用户那里听到的是，他们深陷在音乐品味的"信息茧房"里。我深爱Spotify，也热爱这项服务，但如今我对电子舞曲（EDM）有些腻烦了，而Spotify推荐的内容却始终停留在老套路上。仔细思考这个问题，会发现它与推荐机制的核心矛盾看似相似——毕竟都是推荐系统，但本质上却存在根本差异。例如，当你在EDM播放列表中推荐另一首EDM曲目时，系统已掌握了用户对EDM音乐的偏好信号。但若要推荐完全陌生的音乐类型，系统就完全摸不着头脑——毕竟若你能预测用户喜好，它就不算新奇了。所以在这种情况下，推荐的成功率注定会极低。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So this problem of helping people get out of the taste bubble isn't that easy as it sounds. And we can't really take some genre that maybe isn't typical. So I'm a big fan of Reggaeton, for example. It's not typically ... It's not that common in Sweden. And if you would look the rest of my profile, it's EDM heaviness, you probably wouldn't have guessed it. And Spotify wouldn't have guessed it. So if I'm listening to my favorite EDM playlist in the background or maybe my metal playlist, metal is very big in Sweden, it's really hard for us to just insert a Reggaeton track in the middle of that. Most people are going to think Spotify's broken.
turns.zh: 因此，要帮助人们摆脱音乐口味的"信息茧房"，难度远超想象。我们也不能随便选一些非主流的音乐类型。比如说，我特别喜欢雷鬼顿音乐，但这类音乐在瑞典并不常见。再看看我的个人音乐库，里面全是电子舞曲（EDM）和金属乐，你绝对想不到我还会听雷鬼顿。即便我把雷鬼顿曲目插入EDM播放列表或金属乐播放列表（毕竟金属乐在瑞典很受欢迎），大多数用户也会觉得Spotify出了故障。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: What the hell are they thinking? So that doesn't really work. So in order to help people break out of their taste bubbles, you need something different. You need something where your hit ratio can be very low and you need people to expect it to be very low.
turns.zh: 他们到底在想什么？这样根本行不通。所以，要想帮助人们跳出自己的口味圈，你需要来点不一样的。你需要提供一种成功率极低的推荐机制，而且用户得能预料到这种低成功率的存在。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So when we recommend things in the background, our hit ratio needs to be at least nine out of 10, maybe one dud is okay, but if you get five duds, you're going to think we broke your playlist and your session. We need something where one out of 10 is a success. If you find one gem out of 10 tries, you're very happy. So you need a completely different paradigm. And you also need to be able to go through many candidates quickly because the hit rate is so low. You can't take three minutes per item. It's like, "Okay, I didn't like this," and it's still like two minutes left before the next one comes on. You need to quickly say, "No, no, no." So the obvious candidates for this are these feed-type experience, where you can go through lots of content, you're expecting the hit ratio to be much lower. And if you don't like it, the cost is very low, you just swipe.
turns.zh: 因此，当我们在后台推荐内容时，我们的命中率需要达到至少十分之九。偶尔推荐失败一次或许还能接受，但如果连续五次都推荐失败，你会觉得我们把你的播放列表和使用体验彻底搞砸了。我们需要让每十次推荐中至少有一次成功。如果你十次尝试中能找到一首心仪曲目，你就会非常开心。所以这需要一种完全不同的推荐模式。此外，还必须能快速筛选大量候选内容，因为命中率实在太低了。你不可能对每个推荐都花三分钟时间去仔细评估。比如你听完一首歌觉得不喜欢，再过两分钟下一首歌就来了。你必须迅速做出判断，坚决拒绝不合心意的推荐。显然，适合这种场景的是信息流类体验——用户可以快速浏览大量内容，预期命中率会低很多。即使不喜欢，成本也很低，只需轻轻滑动屏幕即可跳过。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And then this is the reason why people have been ... When they want to break out of their taste bubbles or when they come into Spotify and listen to something completely new, it is usually because they found it on one of these services, like a TikTok or YouTube or something, where they get exposed to lots of new content. So people were asking us for these tools and so that's what we wanted to solve for. And so we built a bunch of features, feed-like structures, where you can go through either a new genre with many tracks or a podcast channel with genre with many episodes or even full playlists. And we implemented those and we put them in something called subfeeds. So in the current experience, and this is roll out worldwide, if you click the podcast subfeed, you get a feed of podcast episodes. Click the music subfeeds, you get a feed of playlists where you can go through many playlists. And if you don't understand the name, you can quickly hear what they sound like and check out a few tracks and understand if this is for you. And if you go through the search and browse page, you can find completely new genres that you can quickly go through.
turns.zh: 接下来，这就是人们一直……当他们想要突破自己的音乐品味圈，或者在Spotify上聆听全新的音乐时，通常是因为他们在TikTok、YouTube等平台上发现了这些内容，在这些平台上，用户能接触到大量新内容。因此，用户们一直向我们呼吁开发相关工具，而这正是我们想要解决的问题。为此，我们开发了一系列功能，打造了类似信息流的结构，用户可以浏览包含多首曲目的新音乐类型、包含多集节目的播客频道，甚至完整的播放列表。我们将这些功能整合到名为"子订阅源"的模块中。在当前全球推出的版本中，用户点击播客子订阅源，即可获取播客剧集的信息流；点击音乐子订阅源，则能看到可供浏览的播放列表。若用户对某个名称不熟悉，还能快速试听其音乐风格，了解是否符合自己的喜好。此外，通过搜索与浏览页面，用户还能发现全新的音乐类型，并快速探索其中的精选内容。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And so those are working as we intended. People go to them when they want to find new music. They browse through them and they save new songs. So they're working as we intended. The thing that didn't work as we intended was when users asked us for this again and again, we took the sum of these things and we put it on Home because people ask so much about discovery and we can see clearly how correlated discoveries with retention on Spotify and so forth. But what we misjudged or failed or rather learned about our own homepage is that the way it works right now, and this is what you can see in the Twitter comment, if you remove the angry voices and try to see what they're saying, they're saying the following, which is actually quite clear in the quantitative data as well, that if you look at what people do on Spotify's homepage, the current one, it is almost 90% what we call recall.
turns.zh: 因此，它们的运作情况完全符合我们的预期。用户想要发现新音乐时，就会去这些板块浏览并收藏新歌曲。它们的功能正如我们所设想的那样。但有一点却未能达到预期——当用户反复向我们提出同样的需求时，我们把这些反馈整合起来，将其纳入了主页板块，因为用户对音乐发现功能的需求实在太高了。我们清楚地看到，音乐发现与用户在Spotify上的留存率等指标之间存在显著关联。但我们低估了主页现有功能的局限性，从Twitter评论中就能看出来——若忽略那些愤怒的质问，仔细解读用户反馈，其实核心诉求很清晰：从量化数据来看，当用户在Spotify现有主页上进行操作时，90%的行为都是我们所说的"回忆式行为"，即用户主动回访、重温过往内容的行为。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So it is either getting to a session that you're already in or a specific playlist that you know you want to get to or at least a specific use case. So you come in with a high intent, you actually knew what you wanted, and maybe only 10% of the time as a true discovery, like I don't know what I want. So if you think about, that is 90% recall and 10% discovery. When we tested the design ... So the subfeeds were working and not working, but when we tested some of them on Home, we switched it from 90/10 to 10/90. So 10% recall, 90% discovery. And while people want discovery, they probably don't want 90% discovery, instead of 90% recall. So if you then look at the comments on Twitter, what they're saying is like, "Hey, I can't find my playlists anymore. Where are these things?"
turns.zh: 也就是说，用户要么是进入一个他们已经加入的会话，要么是找到一个他们明确想听的播放列表，或者至少是某个特定的使用场景。因此，他们进入平台时目标明确，清楚自己想要什么，而真正属于"探索性发现"的情况可能只占10%——比如用户根本不知道自己想听什么。换句话说，用户90%的时间是基于记忆导航，10%的时间是探索发现。在我们测试设计时，子订阅功能时好时坏，但当我们在主界面测试其中一些功能时，比例就从90/10变成了10/90，即用户90%的时间是基于记忆导航，10%的时间是探索发现。虽然用户渴望探索新内容，但他们可能并不希望探索占据全部注意力，而记忆导航才是核心功能。看看推特上的用户评论就知道了，他们普遍抱怨"我找不到自己的播放列表了，这些功能都去哪了？"

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: They're not really complaining about the discovery, they're complaining about the things they don't get anymore. And we can see this in the quant data as well. And you can see traffic shifting from home into search and into library, which is a clear sign people are trying to find the things they can't find anymore. And you can even see people then trying to use these discovery tools which are optimized for quickly understanding new things to do the recall. Where's that workout playlist I know I want? And it's actually very bad UI for recall, it's like a slot machine, right? Very unpredictable if you ever get to that workout playlist. It was optimized for finding new things, not for recall of existing things. When you do recall, you want the dense UI with many items on screen because you know what it is you're looking for. So you don't need a lot of real estate when you're doing discovery of new things. You want a lot of pixels and you probably want sound because you don't know what it is.
turns.zh: 他们实际上并非在抱怨新发现的内容，而是对失去的功能感到不满。从量化数据中我们也能看得清这一点。我们能观察到用户行为从"家庭"界面转向"搜索"和"图书馆"，这清晰表明人们正在努力寻找那些已难以找到的信息。甚至能看到用户试图利用那些专为快速理解新事物而设计的探索工具来进行信息检索——比如"我想找的那份健身播放列表在哪儿？"——但这类界面对于信息检索体验而言实在糟糕，就像老虎机一样难以预测用户能否最终找到想要的信息。这些界面原本是为发现新内容而优化的，而非为检索已有信息而设计。真正进行信息检索时，用户需要密集的界面布局，屏幕上尽可能多地显示相关项目，因为此时用户已经明确知道自己在寻找什么。而在探索新内容时，用户则需要更大的屏幕空间和可能的音频提示，因为他们对目标信息尚不明确。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So what we learn about our UI, and I think there's maybe a little bit of product jealousy here, you always look at other experiences. And if you look around, it could be forgiven for thinking that most other products, if you look at something like YouTube, for example, their homepage is exactly that. It's a huge single-item discovery feed with only new items. And people don't seem to tweet angrily about how angry they are at you to say they love YouTube and it's a big product. And I think what we discovered was that we actually did something really well on our homepage, which was supporting you being inside a multiple sessions at the same time. So you could be in the middle of two podcasts and an audiobook and also them actually I just want to get to that workout playlist. I don't remember the name of it, but I know it's workout.
turns.zh: 那么，我们从用户界面（UI）中学到了什么呢？我觉得这里可能存在些许产品攀比心理——你总会去观察其他产品的体验。环顾四周，你可能会不禁联想到大多数其他产品。比如说YouTube，其主页就是典型例子——一个巨大的单条目发现流，里面全是新内容。人们似乎不会在社交媒体上气急败坏地抱怨YouTube有多棒，称赞它是伟大的产品。通过研究，我们发现我们在主页上做得特别出色的一点，是支持用户同时参与多个会话场景。比如，你可能正在听两期播客和一本有声书，同时又想找到某个健身播放列表。虽然我记不清具体名称，但我知道那是关于健身的。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: We actually did that part really well. I would venture just say much better than the other experiences where you literally have to go to some tab and into library and start browsing to get back to where you were. And so maybe it's path dependent. Because we have done recall pretty well, people got, I think, reasonably upset when they couldn't do the recall anymore. And we didn't want lose that because it was one of the things we did well and underestimated. And my takeaway is actually we do it better than other experiences. So we certainly want to keep that. So what we did was now we're just updating their hypothesis to achieve the same goal, which is these things are working and when people want to discover, they use them and they seem to work, they can also get better.
turns.zh: 实际上，我们在那部分做得非常出色。我敢说，这比其他体验要好得多——在其他体验中，你得专门去某个标签页、进入图书馆并开始浏览，才能回到之前的页面。所以这可能与路径相关。我们在回忆功能上做得很好，当用户无法再使用这个功能时，他们会感到相当不满。我们不想失去这个优势，因为这是我们做得出色却被低估的功能之一。从我的角度来看，我们在这方面确实比其他体验做得更好。所以我们肯定要保留这个功能。现在我们只是在更新他们的假设，以实现同样的目标——这些功能目前运行良好，当用户想要探索新内容时，他们会使用这些功能，而且这些功能似乎还能不断优化。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: You're on this hill-climbing journey from a machine learning point of view, but the question is, how do you make sure that whenever people feel that they are in that I'm trapped in my taste bubble, they understand that these things are there and they're easy to use? So now we have a version of Home that we are also testing, obviously, where these things are very available but voluntary and you can still do all of the recall. And so from my point of view, this is the reason we A/B test because you want to be scientific about it and you want to learn as much as possible about your own product and your users. And now I'm sharing a lot of the learnings. Maybe we should keep them to ourselves, but my hunch is that it's going to make it a much better product.
turns.zh: 从机器学习的角度来看，你正走在攀登这座山峰的征程上。但问题在于，如何确保当人们陷入“被困在自己的口味泡沫中”的困境时，能意识到这些资源的存在并轻松使用它们？目前，我们正在测试的Home版本显然已经提供了这些功能，但它们是自愿参与的，用户仍能完全控制历史记录的回调功能。在我看来，这正是我们进行A/B测试的原因——你需要以科学严谨的态度去优化产品，尽可能深入了解用户需求。现在我要分享许多测试心得。或许我们本该保守这些发现，但直觉告诉我，这样做能让产品变得更加出色。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: But what I told my teams when we went into this, because I've done this a few times, agree to signing, I think there are two fundamentally different types of product development. One is designing a new feature. It is hard, but it's voluntary for people to use. So you do the AI DJ. Some people love it, that's fine. If you don't like it, it didn't make it worse for you. But when you redesign, it is much more tricky because it's not voluntary to participate in the redesign. So there's a cost even for people who don't like it. Then you have a very tricky problem here, which is there are going to be two types of feedback. One is you did something and it was right, but people are upset because you changed stuff. The other is you did something and it wasn't right, and people are also upset but for good reasons.
turns.zh: 但在着手这项工作时，我曾对团队说过——毕竟我亲身经历过多次类似项目——签约合作时，产品开发本质上可以分为两类。一类是设计新功能。这固然困难，但用户可以自主选择是否使用。比如AI DJ功能，有些人喜欢它没问题；不喜欢的话也不会对他们造成实质损害。但当你重新设计产品时，情况就复杂得多——用户被迫参与重构过程，成本不可避免地转嫁到不喜欢新设计的人身上。此时，反馈会出现两种极端情况：一种是产品设计合理，但用户因变更而感到不满；另一种是设计存在缺陷，用户的不满同样合理。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And so how do you separate these two? Because I think I explained this to ... When we talk through this with my teams, I think the analogy to think about is you have your desktop, your physical desktop, you have your computer in one place, you have your pencil over here, you have your notebook over there, and I come in and I just rearrange all of it. And you have spent, in our case, maybe 12 years with that setup. It doesn't matter if I have a lot of quantitative data that my new setup is better, you're going to get upset because you are effective in this old setup. And it's hard to tell those apart. The most classic use case is the Facebook newsfeed, which people are very upset about when it became a single newsfeed. But it turned out to solve a lot of user problems that you didn't have to run around all of Facebook collecting events yourself.
turns.zh: 那么，如何区分这两者呢？因为我觉得我已经解释过这个问题了……当我和团队讨论这个问题时，我认为可以用一个类比来理解：你有自己的桌面——实体桌面——电脑放在一个地方，铅笔放在这边，笔记本放在那边。而我进来后，把所有东西重新整理了一遍。就我们的情况而言，你可能已经习惯了这样的设置12年了。即便我有大量量化数据证明新设置更优，你也会感到不适应，因为你已经在旧设置下高效运作了。要区分这两者确实很难。最典型的例子就是Facebook的新闻推送功能，当它从多个信息流整合为单一推送时，用户们曾非常不满。但最终证明这个设计解决了大量用户痛点——无需再在Facebook上四处搜集各种动态信息。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So there are some ways of understanding if you made it better, but people's habits are broken or if it's not better. And one thing is, for example, to look at new user cohorts that don't have that behavior versus all user cohorts and so forth. So we went through all of this with the teams. Before we did it, I said, "This is going to be painful." There's probably going to be a lot of tweets because chances that we get it exactly right are very low. So for that reason, it hasn't been very hard on the team. It is hard ... You want to respond to people, but the right way to do it is to listen, understand, try new hypothesis to really figure out what's going on. So I think I've done it maybe three or four times now. Three maybe. One unsuccessful, two successfully. So kind of knew what I was getting into.
turns.zh: 因此，要判断你是否真的有所改进，还是用户习惯未变，有几种方法。比如，可以对比新用户群体（没有该行为的用户）和所有用户群体的数据差异。为此，我们和团队仔细研究了所有数据。在开展这项工作前，我曾预警过：“这会很痛苦。”因为要想一次就把所有问题都解决，概率实在太低。所以团队并没有因此感到太大压力。当然，确实存在挑战……你很想回应用户反馈，但正确的做法应该是倾听、理解、尝试新假设，从而真正弄清楚问题根源。到目前为止，我大概尝试过三四次了。其中一次失败了，两次成功了。所以我心里有数，知道自己在做什么。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So it's almost like you punish yourself, very painful, but also the most exciting things. And I think any product person knows that the easiest, the most straightforward thing to do is to iterate around where you are. There's no risk. You're not going to get fired, no user is going to get angry. But everyone also knows that eventually if you don't adapt new technologies, new paradigms, et cetera, you're going to get replaced. You have to find this balance of trying new things. And when you work in software, you have this tool of A/B testing and being scientific about it. When you build hardware, it's worse. If you're wrong, you're wrong. You can't update.
turns.zh: 就好像你在惩罚自己一样，这很痛苦，但同时也是最激动人心的事。我想任何产品从业者都知道，最简单、最直接的做法就是在现有基础上进行迭代。这样既没有风险——你不会被解雇，用户也不会生气——但大家也都清楚，如果不及时适应新技术、新范式等，最终必将被淘汰。你必须在尝试新事物和保持稳健之间找到平衡。而在软件领域，你还有A/B测试这样的工具，可以通过科学的方法验证新方案。但硬件开发就不一样了。一旦决策失误，就只能承担后果，无法回头修改了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this story. I so appreciate you sharing it. I imagine also with a big launch like this, you can't actually A/B test it ahead of time because of the press season. They're like, "Oh my God, look what Spotify's doing." And so you're limited there. Imagine, right? You couldn't really test this ahead of time.
turns.zh: 我超爱这个故事。真心感谢你能分享它。我想像这样的大型发布活动，由于临近宣传季，事先根本没法进行A/B测试。他们肯定会说：“天哪，看看Spotify都做了些什么。”所以在这方面你受到了限制。想想看，对吧？你根本没法提前测试这个方案。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: The hardest thing about this is if you're trying something completely new, the MVP needs to be very big so you can build a new IU, but if you didn't do algorithms for single item feed, you can't tell if it was the right idea but poor machine learning, right? UI poor machine learning. Or you have to build a lot and that gets quite expensive. That's actually ... The biggest why it's painful is not really the feedback from the outside. It is the cost you have to take on the inside. You incur a lot of costs as you're really hoping you're right.
turns.zh: 其中最难的部分在于，如果你要尝试全新的东西，MVP（最小可行产品）规模必须足够大，这样才能构建新的用户界面（UI）。但如果你之前没有做过单品信息流的算法优化，就无法判断这个想法是否正确，只是机器学习做得不好，对吧？UI不行、机器学习不行。要么就得大量开发，但成本会很高。这其实……最让人头疼的不是外部用户的反馈，而是内部需要承担的成本。你会投入大量资源，只为验证自己的假设是否正确。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And in our cases, the changes on the homepage aren't that hard for us to do. The important thing is that the underlying hypothesis of, can we help you break out of your taste bubble actually works and then you update the acquisition funnels into that experience. But I think the problem is that you need to get so many things in place to be able to say, "You might get a false negative," just because you didn't do it well or not. That's the biggest challenge, I think, with these big rewrites where everyone has to update everything before you can know if you're right or wrong.
turns.zh: 就我们的情况而言，主页上的改动对我们来说并不难。关键在于，"我们能否帮助你突破口味偏好圈"这个核心假设是否有效，然后将获取用户的漏斗机制升级到符合这一体验的标准。但我认为最大的挑战在于，要想准确判断"你可能遭遇了误判"——无论是因为操作不当还是其他原因——你需要先把所有环节都准备到位。这种大规模的重构工作，所有人都得先完成所有更新，才能判断自己做得对不对，这无疑是最大的挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What was that process like of helping you understand what is not working and what is working and what you wanted to change? I imagine there's a bunch of data you're looking at, some tweets, things like that. What was the tactical, "Oh, shoot, something's not going the way we expected, here's what we should do?"
turns.zh: 帮助你理解哪些地方做得不好，哪些地方做得好，还有你想要做出哪些改变，这个过程是怎样的？我猜你需要分析大量数据，比如推文之类的。有没有那种战术性的时刻——"哎呀，情况不像我们预期的那样，接下来该怎么做？"

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Well, the feeds, we tested, but the home feed, we rolled out and tested afterwards. And we tested out on users, a few different variants of it. And then we got the data back and we looked more at the quantitative data. And we do a lot of user research where people sit and use the feeds to understand and build our own theorem mind of what is working and what is not working. And then, obviously, you look at user feedback, of course, and some users are very good at expressing what is of it that isn't working, others are not as good as expressing what isn't working. So it can be hard to parse that, but certainly, that's a factor as well.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们对推送内容进行了测试，但主页推送功能是在上线后才进行测试的。我们向用户推送了几个不同版本的推送内容，收集了数据后又仔细分析了定量数据。我们还开展了大量用户研究，让用户实际使用推送功能，以此来理解并构建我们自己的推送逻辑，判断哪些设计有效，哪些无效。当然，我们也会参考用户反馈。有些用户善于指出推送内容的不足，而有些用户则不太善于表达问题。因此，解析这些反馈可能存在困难，但用户反馈无疑也是一个关键考量因素。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: And so then once you do that, then you have quantitative data to look at. And then you sit in recent through, what do you think is right and wrong? What are the different hypotheses? What is working, what is not working? And then just update and test again and again until you prove or disprove your hypothesis. Trying to be as scientific as possible about it. And also I think the biggest risk also when you've invested so much time in something is getting precious about things. You have to just be brutal. You have to believe in things 100% until the data says no and then you believe in something else 100%. That sounds easy. It's very hard to do, to the extent that people get upset when you do it because, for some reason, people don't like when people change their minds. It is what we should want from everyone. I would love a politician who said, "I'd looked at the data and I realized actually this is right and now I believe this." But we hate politicians that do that. They feel untrustworthy and we ridicule them.
turns.zh: 接下来，一旦你完成了这些步骤，就能获得可量化的数据进行分析。然后，你要坐下来仔细思考：哪些做法是对的，哪些是错的？有哪些不同的假设？哪些方法有效，哪些无效？接着不断更新并反复验证，直到证明或推翻你的假设。整个过程要尽可能保持科学严谨。同时，我认为在投入大量时间后，最大的风险就是对某些事物产生执着依恋。你必须保持冷静，百分百坚信某个观点直到数据反驳，再转而相信新的结论。这听起来简单，但实施起来却极其困难。人们往往会对这种改变主意的行为感到不满，因为出于某种原因，他们不喜欢别人改变立场。但这恰恰是我们希望每个人都能做到的。我倒希望有政客能说：“我研究了数据，发现这个观点是正确的，现在我坚信这一点。”但我们却对这样做的人心存偏见，认为他们不可信，甚至加以嘲笑。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So I think that's the biggest risk with anyone. You just have to be unemotional and just look at the proof and the data. And then if you do that, you just move on and then you get to where you want to be, and you solve the same problem but you adapt.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得这才是面对任何人时最大的风险所在。你只需要保持冷静，专注于证据和数据。这样做之后，你就能继续前进，最终到达你想去的地方。虽然解决的是同一个问题，但你需要灵活应变，调整方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really like that philosophy. Essentially, it's the idea of strong opinions loosely held. Is that-
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢这种哲学。简单来说，就是持有坚定信念但又不拘泥于教条的理念。您觉得呢？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Exactly. Exactly what it is. And it sounds so easy, but it's hard.
turns.zh: 没错。就是这么回事儿。听起来挺简单，但做起来可难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right? Because to your point, people don't respect someone changing their mind. They're like, "Oh, I see, they were wrong the whole time and they were so confident about being wrong."
turns.zh: 是吧？因为说真的，人们并不尊重那些改变主意的人。他们会觉得：“哦，原来他们一直都错了，可他们还那么自信地坚持错误观点呢。”

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And it's unclear why it is what we should want, but I think it has something to do with human psychology. We actually tend to love profits and people who hold very strong opinions with very little data. Those are the people we like. People will look at a lot of data and actually that, we don't like. Not sure why.
turns.zh: 是啊，说得没错。为什么我们会希望如此呢？这背后可能与人类心理学有关。我们往往更青睐那些热衷于追逐利润、在掌握极少数据的情况下就形成坚定观点的人——这类人更容易赢得我们的好感。相反，当人们在充分研究数据后得出结论时，我们却往往不买账。真不知道这是为什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're flawed creatures.
turns.zh: 人类本就是不完美的。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: For sure.
turns.zh: 肯定啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something that you've recently changed your mind about along these same lines that maybe comes to mind of like, "Oh, yeah?"
turns.zh: 最近有没有什么事让你改变了看法？类似这样的情况，你有没有突然灵光一闪，心里默默想：“哦，对啊！”的那种感觉？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: No, I think these learnings about the science system and homepage does really well, maybe better than others, that we don't want to wash out with a bath water or whatever the [inaudible 01:02:20] expression is. I think that's the biggest current learning I'm actually very happy about.
turns.zh: 不是的，我觉得我们在科学体系和主页方面的这些探索做得非常出色，可能比其他平台做得更好。我们不想因为一时冲动就把这些成果全盘否定，或者用那句"一桶冷水浇灭热情"之类的俗语来形容。我认为这是目前最重要的收获，我对此感到非常欣慰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I love learning that we're doing some really well that we didn't really realize necessarily and maybe we should lead into that more.
turns.zh: 是啊，我很高兴得知我们在某些方面做得相当出色，而这些成果我们可能并未充分意识到，或许我们应该更多地向外界宣传一下我们的成就。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Going in a somewhat different direction. Shishir Mehrotra suggested to ask you something. He's on your board, I believe.
turns.zh: 换个稍微不同的方向。希希尔·梅赫罗特拉建议问你个问题。我想他是你们董事会成员吧。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And he suggested to ask you about your 10% planning time. What is that about?
turns.zh: 然后他建议向你询问关于你那10%的规划时间的事。这是怎么回事呢？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: This is a concept that I think Shishir has used for a long time ever since he worked at YouTube. And the idea is that, roughly, you shouldn't be spending more than 10% of your time planning versus executing or building, which means that if you're working quarterly 10 weeks, you should spend one week planning as we work in six-month increment. So we try to spend two weeks planning and roughly successful. And this is ... Actually, when we talk about org models, give a shout-out to Brian Chesky at Airbnb, who is actually one of the first, I think, to have these more contrarian old models. He's much more applesque than most of Silicon Valley. He also works in six-month increments. He has a lot of experience in that as well. So that's what the 10% planning time is. And I think if you find yourself planning much more than that, you're either planning too much or your execution period is just too short for that amount of planning. It's a rule of thumb, but I find that it works.
turns.zh: 这是一个我认为希希尔自从在YouTube工作以来就一直秉持的理念。大致来说，规划的时间不应超过执行或构建时间的10%。比如说，如果你的季度工作周期是10周，那么你应该用一周时间进行规划（因为我们以六个月为增量周期）。所以我们通常会花两周时间进行规划，并取得不错的成效。说到组织架构模式，这里要特别提一下Airbnb的布莱恩·切斯基。他可以说是最早提出这些非传统模式的人之一。他比大多数硅谷人士更像乔布斯式的人物。他的工作周期同样以六个月为单位，在这方面经验丰富。这就是规划时间占10%的原因。我觉得如果你发现自己花在规划上的时间远超这个比例，要么是规划过度，要么是执行周期太短，无法支撑如此多的规划。这只是个经验法则，但我发现它确实有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I asked a few PMs what I should ask you, PMs that work at Spotify actually, that I haven't told you. And someone pointed out that you always bring a lot of energy and clarity to a room. That's something they see you as really strong at. What have you learned about just the importance of that or just how to do that well as a leader?
turns.zh: 我问过几位项目经理（PM）该问你些什么——都是在Spotify工作的PM，之前没跟你提过这事儿。有人指出，你总能为会议注入满满的活力和清晰思路。这是他们认为你特别擅长的地方。作为领导者，你对这种能力的重要性有何深刻认识？或者说，你是如何把这项技能做得如此出色的？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Well, that's great to hear. I didn't know that so I'm trying to figure out what to answer. I think that the energy, I don't know. I guess I'm just excited about what I do. I've always been excited about technology. I love seeing new things. My core drive is still this notion of you see something which I think you'll empathize with that doesn't exist yet. And you're like, "Wow, I wonder if that could exist. That would be so cool." And then in order to get people to do it, you try to share that excitement. So I don't think I can bring a lot of energy for something I'm not excited about. So I have to work on things I actually believe in and that I'm excited about. And so maybe then the energy comes more naturally. Unfortunately, for me, so far, Spotify has been in this phase where a lot of innovation is allowed and I'm even asked to try to do new cool things.
turns.zh: 嗯，听到你这么说真是太好了。我之前并不知道这些情况，所以我现在正绞尽脑汁想该怎么回答。我觉得可能是因为我对自己所做的事充满热情吧。我一直对科技充满热情，喜欢探索新事物。我的核心驱动力仍然是——当你看到一些你认为会引起共鸣但尚未存在的东西时，会不由自主地惊呼：“哇，这东西要是能实现该多酷啊！”然后，为了让别人也感受到这种激情，你就得努力把这份热情传递出去。所以对于那些我不感兴趣的事，我是很难投入太多精力的。所以我必须专注于自己真正相信且充满热情的项目。这样或许热情就能自然而然地产生了。但很遗憾的是，到目前为止，Spotify还处于一个允许大量创新、甚至鼓励尝试新酷事物的阶段。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Maybe I would have less energy for a pure optimization phase. On the clarity, I've always liked trying to explain things. It's a well-known fact that the best way to understand something is to try to explain to someone else. So I go around explaining things to people who didn't ask for it and not to sound smart, but to see if I actually understood it. And so maybe it's that practice. And on that note, I actually do ask my leaders that work for me and I ask them to ask their leaders to always explain themselves. And I think when ... We talked a little bit about autonomy and so forth, we don't promise everyone that they have to agree, but I think the promise we should make to all employees is that even if they don't agree, they should be entitled to understand why you're making the decision.
turns.zh: 或许我没有足够的精力投入纯粹的优化阶段。说到清晰表达，我一直乐于尝试把事情讲清楚。众所周知，理解某件事的最佳方法就是尝试向他人解释。因此，我会主动向那些并未主动求教的人讲解相关内容——并非为了显摆，而是想验证自己是否真的理解了相关知识。或许这就是一种刻意练习吧。顺便说一句，我确实会要求手下员工的领导们，让他们也去要求自己的下属时刻保持清晰的沟通。正如我们之前讨论过自主权等话题时，我们并不会承诺所有人都必须认同某个决策，但我认为我们应该向所有员工作出这样的承诺：即使他们不认同你的决定，他们也理应有权了解你做出该决定的缘由。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: What I don't think is acceptable is to say, "No, we're going to do it this way because I'm more senior. I've seen this a bunch of times. You are not smart enough." All of those things. I think you have to explain yourself so you owe an explanation. And I find that valuable back to the only way to understand something is to explain it because it usually turns out that if you can't explain it yourself, you probably don't really even understand it yourself. Sometimes I think it's possible that you can have product instincts that are good but you can't express them. But most of them, when people say there's something there but they can't explain it, they actually don't understand it themselves. And many times, there actually isn't anything there. And also if you can explain it as a product person, that knowledge is now shared. So it just becomes much more effective for the organization. So sometimes I try to provoke people a little bit and say ... When people ask how much is art versus science, I say, "It's 0% art, 0% magic, and 100% science." And that's because I want to force people to try to explain it. I think we use the word art and magic. We have historically used the word art and magic for anything that we couldn't yet explain.
turns.zh: 我认为不可接受的是说"不，我们要按我的方式来做，因为我资历更深。我见过太多次这种情况了。你不够聪明。"诸如此类的话。我觉得你得给出解释——你有义务说明理由。回到我之前的观点：理解事物唯一的途径就是把它解释清楚，因为如果你自己都无法解释清楚，那说明你根本没真正理解它。有时你可能有不错的产品直觉，但无法清晰表达。但大多数情况下，当人们声称"这里有东西"却无法解释时，其实他们自己根本不明白。而很多时候，根本就没什么东西可解释的。此外，如果你能以产品从业者的身份把它解释清楚，知识就能被共享。这样对整个组织的效益会大得多。所以有时我会故意激怒别人说：……当人们问"艺术与科学的比例是多少"时，我会回答"艺术占0%，魔法占0%，科学占100%。"这样做是为了迫使人们尝试解释。我认为我们常用"艺术"和"魔法"这类词汇。历史上，我们用这两个词来形容那些尚未能被解释清楚的事物。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Genetics was magic and art until it was science. And quantum physics was magic until it was science. And most recently, actually, intelligence and creativity was art and magic until it was statistics in an LLM. So I think I try to push people to say, "Are you sure you can explain this?" because that forces people to think through. So maybe I like it and I try to force it on people. So maybe that's why people think I sometimes bring clarity.
turns.zh: 基因学在成为科学之前曾是魔法与艺术，量子物理学在成为科学之前同样是魔法。而最近，智能与创造力在成为法学硕士课程中的统计学对象之前，也同样是艺术与魔法。因此，我总会试着促使人们反问：“你确定能解释清楚吗？”这样能迫使他们进行深度思考。或许我乐于如此，喜欢将这种思维方式强加于人。所以，或许这就是人们觉得我有时能让复杂问题变得清晰易懂的原因吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Question along those lines, is there a system or an approach to explaining that you recommend? Is it just write it out in a document? Is it explaining in a certain style or is it just however is natural to the person?
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这样。顺便问一下，对于如何解释这个问题，你有什么推荐的体系或方法吗？是直接写成文档吗？还是用某种特定的表达方式？或者就按照说话者最自然的方式来解释？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I used to write everything and then write and rewrite and make it more and more condensed. So that worked for me. I don't write as much anymore. Now, I tend to walk and talk in my head myself. What I actually do is I ... And I found this different for different people and a lot of people want to bounce something with someone else, that's how they think. You repeat the same thing again and again and you get some feedback on it. And so I used to write a lot. I sometimes do when it's an idea I want to understand better. And at some point in my life, I would love to write something real like a book or something. But what I do increasingly now is I do my one-on-ones with peers or people who report to me or something, and I just put on AirPods and do a distributed walk and talk.
turns.zh: 我过去常常把所有东西都写下来，然后反复修改，使内容越来越简洁。这对我很有效。不过现在我写作得少多了。现在，我更倾向于边走路边在脑海中构思。实际上，我会……我发现不同的人有不同的习惯，很多人喜欢和别人交流想法，这样能获得反馈。我过去写作很多，有时当我想更深入理解某个想法时，还是会动笔写作。人生某个阶段，我很想写一本真正的书之类的东西。但现在我越来越多地与同事、下属等进行一对一交流时，会戴上AirPods，边走路边思考问题。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Both people are walking but in different locations and you spend an hour discussing something. That has actually turned out to be very, very fruitful. So then you get the power of you're not alone so you get more brain power than your own. And I don't think there is strong evolutionary proof for this, but there's certainly indications that you're thinking better when you're walking, whether it's because you're oxygenating your brain or because it's evolutionary for some other reason, I'm not sure. But I found that walking, talking, and thinking actually even if you're not in person, just over AirPods, it's super effective. It was the pandemic that forced us. I thought we would get less creative and strategizing will suffer during the pandemic and I found the opposite. We had more of this than ever and I started thinking about why, and I think it's all of these walk and talks that we did.
turns.zh: 两个人虽然身处不同地点，但都在行走中，并且花了一个小时讨论某个话题。结果证明这次交流收获颇丰。这种交流能激发智慧火花，让你获得比独自思考更强大的思维力量。虽然目前尚无强有力的进化论据支持这一观点，但确实有迹象表明，行走时思考效率更高——无论是因为大脑得到了充足氧气，还是出于其他进化原因，我尚不确定。但我发现，即便无法当面交流，仅通过AirPods通话边走边聊，也能达到超乎想象的效果。正是疫情期间的居家隔离，迫使我们不得不另辟蹊径。我原本以为疫情会降低我们的创造力和战略规划能力，但结果恰恰相反。反而是那段时期，我们开展了比以往更多的边走边聊的深度对话，这或许正是创造力激增的根本原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You threw out there that you want to write a book someday. What do you think your book would be about?
turns.zh: 你之前提到过希望将来写一本书。你觉得你的书会是关于什么内容的呢？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I have no idea. I have no idea. Statistically, it's probably going to be about something that I did a lot, so it has to be about something with technology or product or something. But I would love to write something fictional. That'd be a lot of fun.
turns.zh: 我不知道。我不知道。从统计学角度看，很可能是关于我常做的事情，所以肯定和科技、产品之类的相关。但我倒是挺想写点虚构类的东西，那应该会很有趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, boy. I'll pre-order as soon as that's up. Another concept I wanted to touch on that another PM suggested, which is he called it the P in the pants analogy. Does that ring a bell? And is that interesting to talk about?
turns.zh: 天哪。这东西一上线我就去预订了。还有个概念我想提一下，之前另一位产品经理提过，他把这叫做"裤子里的P"这个比喻。你们有没有听过这个说法？聊聊这个有意思吗？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I don't know exactly which occasion this person is referring to, but I know I've used that analogy a few times.
turns.zh: 我不确定对方具体指的是哪种场合，但我知道自己曾多次用过这个比喻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Promising.
turns.zh: 好的。听起来不错。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I don't know if it's like a Swedish analogy because I thought it was more widely known. But the idea is that you do something ... So the saying is that's like peeing in your pants in cold weather. It feels really warm and nice to begin with. And then after a while, you start to regret it. It's about being short term, basically. So now I just say that's like peeing in the pants inside because people know what I mean. It's a short-term thing.
turns.zh: 我不知道这是否是瑞典的比喻，因为我原以为它更广为人知。但这个说法的意思是，你做某件事……就像在寒冷的天气里尿裤子一样。一开始会觉得很温暖舒适，但过一段时间后，你就会开始后悔。这基本上就是短视行事的意思。所以现在我直接说"就像在屋里尿裤子"，这样大家就明白我的意思了。这就是短视的表现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a hilarious way of communicating that idea. Must be a Swedish thing.
turns.zh: 用这种方式传达这个想法真是太搞笑了。看来这应该是瑞典人的一贯作风吧。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Yes, I think Swedish people do it for some reason, apparently others don't.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得瑞典人会这么做，显然其他国家的人却不这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe because it's cold a lot of times of the year.
turns.zh: 或许是因为一年中有很多时候天气寒冷吧。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Yes. That's probably it. This is a saying in cold climate. In the warm, it doesn't help. No one understands what you mean.
turns.zh: 是啊，大概就是这样。这是寒冷气候地区的一句谚语。在温暖的地方，这话可不管用——没人能理解你想表达的意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of Sweden, do you watch Succession?
turns.zh: 说到瑞典，你看《继承者们》这部剧吗？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Yes, I do.
turns.zh: 是的，我确实有。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So Sweden's become a big part of the show, specifically the company trying to ... I guess I don't want to spoil, but there's a character that's really important. Yes, exactly. That is Swedish. And so I'm curious just what do you think of the way they portray the Swedish culture and Swedish business dealings?
turns.zh: 好的。瑞典在剧中占据了重要地位，尤其是那家试图……嗯，我不想剧透，但有个角色确实至关重要。没错，就是瑞典人。我很好奇，你觉得剧中对瑞典文化和瑞典商业往来的刻画如何？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: It's super fun to see this as a Sweden. And I guess, first and foremost, like anyone or any person or any country that gets represented by super tall, well-built, great looking Alexander Skarsgård should probably be pretty happy. So that's good. Then I think there's this episode where they are in Norway, without giving away too much.
turns.zh: 看到瑞典以亚历山大·斯卡斯加德这样高大英俊的形象亮相，真是太有趣了。我想，首先，任何被亚历山大·斯卡斯加德这样高大帅气的形象所代表的人或国家，都应该感到无比自豪。这确实很棒。然后，我记得有一集他们去了挪威，不过我不想剧透太多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: There are elements that are authentic. There's a lot of, I think, paid brand positioning from a Swedish brand named Fjällräven, which I think means arctic fox, which is actually a very popular outdoor brand in Sweden. So that's authentic. The sauna things and so forth are authentic. So it's real, but it's exaggerated. Actually, the thing that isn't very authentic is his negotiation style. Swedish people tend to be serious, cautious, and this guy's more of a player. So he's not the typical Swedish businessman from a negotiation tactic point of view, I think.
turns.zh: 有些元素是真实的。比如，瑞典品牌Fjällräven（我认为这个名字意为"北极狐"）在品牌定位上投入了大量资金推广。这家品牌实际上是瑞典非常受欢迎的户外品牌，所以这部分是真实的。桑拿房之类的场景也比较贴切。但整体而言，影片中的某些元素虽然真实，却被夸大了。实际上最不真实的部分是他谈判的风格。瑞典人通常比较严谨、谨慎，而这个角色更像个投机取巧的人。从谈判策略的角度来看，他显然不符合瑞典商人的典型形象。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it doesn't make me think of the way you described it where in Sweden, people sit in a circle and no one's in the center.
turns.zh: 是啊，但这和我想象的瑞典场景不太一样——在瑞典，人们通常围成一圈坐着，中间不会有空位。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: No, exactly. He's very much in the center.
turns.zh: 没错，就是这样。他在聚光灯下备受瞩目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then when people go saunas, there are just like a chant, sauna, sauna [inaudible 01:13:23].
turns.zh: 然后当人们去桑拿房时，那里总会有人反复念叨着“桑拿，桑拿”之类的话。[01:13:23，语音不清晰]。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The last episode.
turns.zh: 最后一集。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: It's a great show. I love it.
turns.zh: 这是一部很棒的剧集。我超爱它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. This season is insane. I'm so curious where it all goes. Maybe just the last question before very exciting lightning round. Spotify is, at this point, the biggest podcasting platform for me specifically and I think globally, and I love using it. It works great. I'm curious just what's next for Spotify and specifically Spotify podcasting.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。这一季简直太疯狂了。我很好奇整个剧情会如何发展。在即将到来的激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，或许先回答最后一个问题。就我个人而言，Spotify目前是最大的播客平台，我相信在全球范围内也是如此，我非常喜欢使用它。它的运行效果非常出色。我很好奇Spotify以及其播客业务接下来的发展方向。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: There are two sides to it. It's for Spotify creators and for Spotify listeners. For Spotify creators, there are two things. One is, and this is what we talked about at Stream On, we talked about it also for music discovery, but it's the same problem and even harder for podcast. So we're still focused very heavily on helping podcast creators find more audience. This is ... Like I said, it's even a bigger problem to break out of your habits and your bubbles in podcasting. Such a big investment to find a new podcast. And so that is something, I think, we could and should do really well. So we keep investing a lot there. And as I said, you'll see more as we roll up more features now.
turns.zh: 事情有两方面。一个是针对Spotify创作者，另一个是针对Spotify听众。对于Spotify创作者而言，有两个重点。首先，正如我们在Stream On大会上所讨论的，音乐发现固然重要，但对于播客而言，这个问题更为严峻。因此，我们仍在大力帮助播客创作者拓展受众群体。正如我所说，要突破播客领域的固有思维模式和信息茧房，难度远超音乐领域。用户需要投入大量精力才能发现新的播客内容。所以我认为，在这方面我们完全有能力且应当做得更好。目前我们持续投入大量资源，随着更多功能的上线，大家很快就能看到更显著的成果。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: The other big need for creators is monetization and you can monetize today in many ways with DEI and Spotify SEI and so forth. But we're working hard to expand that and make it better because the industry is starting to mature and I think this is one of the biggest needs and the biggest things we could do for creators to help them monetize better, actually both free and paid. We also have paid podcast. So that's on the creator side.
turns.zh: 创作者的另一大需求是变现。如今，通过DEI、Spotify SEI等平台，创作者可以通过多种方式实现收益。但我们正在努力拓展和优化相关服务，因为整个行业正日益成熟。我认为，这正是创作者最迫切的需求之一，也是我们能为他们提供的最大助力——帮助他们更好地实现免费和付费内容的变现。例如，我们还推出了付费播客服务。这就是我们在创作者端所做的努力。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: On the consumer side, I don't want to share too much. We've shown that we're investing a lot in discovery. I want to keep some secrets for when they roll out, but we are investing a lot in the user expense itself. I think it's far from optimal yet what it could be. One thing that I can share that we're investing a lot in is just the ubiquity and playback across different devices and in cars and all these things that we've done well for music. But I think the listening experience can get a lot more seamless. I think search can get better. The data about podcasts and ... Well, I don't want to say too much, but looking at AI and generative technology, there is a lot that can be done.
turns.zh: 就消费者端而言，我不想透露太多信息。我们已表明正大力投入探索领域。我想保留一些新功能上线时的惊喜，但我们确实在用户体验本身上投入了大量资源。目前的成果尚未达到理想状态。不过有一点我可以透露——我们正大力优化跨设备、车载等场景的无缝播放体验，这方面我们在音乐领域已取得显著成果。但我认为收听体验仍有巨大优化空间，搜索功能也可进一步提升。关于播客数据……嗯，我不想过多透露，但从人工智能和生成式技术的角度来看，还有诸多可优化之处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right. Well, I'll take what I can get. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you, Gustav. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好吧，那我就见好就收了。接下来是我们激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有六个问题要问你，古斯塔夫。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I think I am. Let's do it.
turns.zh: 我觉得我可以。走起吧！

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, we'll find out. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的，我们来了解一下。你向别人推荐过最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Okay. This is why I try to squeeze in seven into two and three. So if we start on product, I think it's well known, but one that I would recommend product people to read is 7 Powers by Hamilton Helmer, and Netflix has used a lot. We use a lot. It's just if you're starting out, it's great to have a strategy framework. No strategy framework is right, but having one is better than none.
turns.zh: 好的。这就是为什么我试图把七个要点浓缩成两到三个部分。那么，如果我们从产品方面入手，我认为这本书广为人知，但我强烈推荐产品从业者阅读汉密尔顿·赫尔默的《7种力量》。这本书在Netflix内部被广泛应用，我们公司也经常参考它。尤其是对于初入行的人来说，拥有一个战略框架至关重要。虽然没有完美的战略框架，但总比没有强。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Another in the space of mental models and frameworks, I think, is The Complete Investor by Charlie Munger. So, yes, it's about investment, but really it's a bunch of mental models that he uses. And I think the key takeaway is you have a problem, you should always apply three different models to it because what models do is they simplify and reduce dimensionality. The world has probably infinite dimensions and they reduces to maybe three or four. And the risk with that is you happen to get rid of a really important dimension, maybe pandemic diseases or something. But if you use three models that have different dimensions and was reduced in different ways, statistically, and it comes to the same conclusion, even the second model you apply vastly increases your chances that you're right. So that was a good book to read.
turns.zh: 关于心智模型和思维框架的书籍，查理·芒格的《完整投资者》（The Complete Investor）也是一本佳作。虽然这本书主要讲投资，但核心内容其实是他所运用的各种心智模型。我认为最重要的启示是：当你遇到问题时，应该用三种不同的模型去分析它。这些模型能够简化复杂性，降低维度数。世界本质上是无限维度的，但模型会将其浓缩为三四个维度。但这样做存在风险——你可能会忽略掉某个关键维度，比如疫情爆发之类的不可预测因素。但如果你使用三个不同维度、以不同方式简化后的模型，通过统计方法得出相同结论，那么第二个模型的加入就能大大提高你做出正确判断的概率。所以这本书值得一读。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Then I think if we go outside of product, I'm very interested in just science and mathematics. So a few quick ones. The Mystery of the Aleph, an amazing book. Something Deeply Hidden by Sean Carroll on the interpretation of quantum mechanics. Helgoland by Carlo Rovelli on the relational interpretation of quantum mechanics. The Beginning of Infinity and The Fabric of Reality by David Deutch. The Case Against Reality by Donald Hoffman on the evolution versus truth and that evolution doesn't optimize for seeing the truth, just for fitness. Gödel's Proof, I think, is an amazing book on his incompleteness theorem, that in any axiomatic systems, there will be true statements that can never be proven, which is a weird thing to think about. And then maybe one of my favorites is The Demon in the Machine by Paul Davies that, I think, is lesser known on how information is really just entropy and this concept of information engines, that you can power something by just information and exhaust is also information. That was not a quick list.
turns.zh: 接下来，我觉得如果不谈产品方面的话，我对科学和数学非常感兴趣。简单列举几本精彩之作：《阿莱夫之谜》——一本令人惊叹的著作；肖恩·卡罗尔的《深藏之物》——关于量子力学诠释的佳作；卡洛·罗维利的《赫尔戈兰岛》——从关联性角度解读量子力学；大卫·多伊奇的《无穷的起源》和《现实的结构》；唐纳德·霍夫曼的《反现实》——探讨进化与真理的关系，指出进化并非为了洞察真相而优化，而只是为了生存；哥德尔证明——解析他的不完备性定理，指出在任何公理化系统中，都存在无法证明的真命题，这真是个令人费解的概念；保罗·戴维斯的《机器中的恶魔》——这本鲜为人知的著作，阐释了信息本质上是熵的概念，并提出了信息引擎的理论，即仅靠信息就能驱动事物运转，且排放物同样是信息。这还不是一份完整的书单呢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I was just going to say you've set the record for the most number of books, but it also shows how you've become so insightful and wise just reading books like these. And so I think if people are looking to get to a place that you're at now, I think there's the lesson.
turns.zh: 不是，我刚想说你创下了阅读书籍数量最多的纪录，但这也表明，仅仅通过阅读这类书籍，你就变得如此有洞察力和智慧。所以我认为，如果有人想达到你现在所处的境界，我觉得这里面有值得借鉴的地方。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I'll keep the artist much shorter, I promise.
turns.zh: 我保证以后会把艺术家介绍得简洁多了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's all good. We got time. Okay, next question. What's a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 没关系，我们还有时间。好的，下一个问题。你最近最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So we talked about Succession and it is a recent favorite. So I'll just frivolously take something that isn't recent but is an absolute favorite, which is Halt and Catch Fire, which I think is on FX. Amazing show. If you ever worked in technology, kind of starts out in the Silicon Prairie in the '80s and follows up to present day. Amazing show.
turns.zh: 于是我们聊起了《继承之战》，这部剧最近成了我的心头好。我就随便说说另一部虽然不算新作但绝对堪称经典的剧集——《黑客军团》，我记得它是在FX电视台播出的。这部剧太棒了。如果你曾在科技行业工作过，就会知道它以80年代的"硅草原"为背景，故事一直延续到当下，堪称一部令人惊叹的佳作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Halt and Catch Fire. Yeah, I watched some of it. I actually fell off of it, but it's a good reminder to go check it out.
turns.zh: 《止损与反击》。嗯，我看过几集这个剧。说实话，我后来没再追下去了，但现在想起来还是挺值得一看的。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Got to go back.
turns.zh: 得回去了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to go back. What's a favorite recent interview question you like to ask?
turns.zh: 我要回去了。你最近最喜欢问的一个面试问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I don't ask it, but my favorite question is Lex Fridman's small ending question that is usually something like, so what's the meaning of it all? I like that. It's a tough question to get.
turns.zh: 我倒不常问这个问题，不过我最喜欢的提问是莱克斯·弗里德曼（Lex Fridman）在节目结尾时抛出的那个小问题——通常会问"那么这一切的意义何在？"我很喜欢这个问题。要想得到这样的深刻见解，可不容易啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm so tempted to ask you, but-
turns.zh: 我真想问问你，但——

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: No, don't.
turns.zh: 别这样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let's move on. That'll be another ... That'll be our second take at this.
turns.zh: 好的。我们继续吧。再来一遍……这将是我们这段内容的第二次拍摄了。

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some favorite products you've recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 最近你发现了哪些自己特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: The obvious one is ChatGPT GPT-4 and just playing around with that, trying to create bots for yourself that do different things for you and so forth. But I don't think that's probably true for everyone. The other really favorite is something you've written about and talked about, which is Duolingo, which I think is both very impressive from a product point of view, the execution and what they've done. It is also insanely used in my family. We have a family account and everyone is using it and competing every day. So I'm both impressed by the product and I also use the product quite a lot.
turns.zh: 显而易见的例子是ChatGPT和GPT-4，我自己也经常把玩它们，试图为自己创建能完成各种任务的机器人之类的。但我觉得这可能并非适用于所有人。另一个我特别喜欢的应用是Duolingo，你之前也写过相关内容并多次提及它。从产品角度来看，我认为Duolingo在执行力和功能设计上都非常出色。它在我的家庭中也被疯狂使用——我们开设了家庭账户，每个人每天都在使用它互相竞赛。所以我既对这款产品印象深刻，自己也经常使用它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What languages are folks learning within your family?
turns.zh: 你们家里的成员都在学习哪些语言呢？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: In my family, it's Spanish right now.
turns.zh: 在我家，现在流行说西班牙语。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How's it going?
turns.zh: 最近怎么样啊？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: Bien.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You get a gold star.
turns.zh: 你真棒，值得表扬！

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I only have a few thousand XP. I'm not that good yet.
turns.zh: 我只有几千点经验值。我的技术还不够好呢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No, I don't know if that's good. That sounds pretty good. Next question, what's something relatively minor you've changed in your product development process that's had a tremendous impact on your team's ability to execute?
turns.zh: 哦，不知道这样做是否合适。不过听起来倒是个不错的主意。接下来我想问，您在产品开发流程中做过哪些相对微小的改进，却对团队执行能力产生了巨大影响？

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: I'm not sure I've done anything minor that had a tremendous impact. Usually, it takes something bigger to get a big impact. I think maybe one thing that I've tried to do back to clarity and so forth is this thing I mentioned about I'm trying to push a lot for what I call Socratic debate, where the idea is obviously that the best idea wins, not the most senior idea and so forth. And trying to push for this notion of having people explain themselves, not saying I think there's something there or have a feeling or something like that. And apparently, as you said, that has had some impact because people apparently say that about me. So that's probably the biggest thing.
turns.zh: 我不确定自己是否做过什么微不足道却产生巨大影响的事。通常，要产生重大影响需要更重大的行动。我想，或许我曾努力做过一件事——那就是回归清晰的思维方式等等。我一直在大力推广我所谓的"苏格拉底式辩论"，其核心理念显然是以最佳观点取胜，而非以资历最深者的意见为准。我努力倡导让人们清晰阐述自己的观点，避免轻易下结论、凭感觉做判断之类的。显然，正如你所说，此举产生了一定影响，因为人们似乎会这样评价我。所以这或许是我做过的最重要的事了。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Gustav Söderström
turns.en: So Spotify is so big now that it's quite local actually, different parts of Spotify, different product rituals. I accidentally created one ritual many years ago, maybe 12 years ago, when we talked about which phase a product is in. And it was ... We needed some definition. So I think off the cuff, I said, "Well, it's four phases." It's think it, build it, ship it, tweak it." And then the think it phase, it should be cheap, not a lot of money spent. In the build it phase, you're going to start spending a lot of money. So then you must have reduced the risk in the think it phase that you're right. And then you have the ship it phase and then you go over and tweak it. And it was something that wasn't that thought through, but it's funny because I still hear it sometimes even from other companies like, "Oh, we're in the think it phase," or "We're in the tweak it phase." So it stuck. I don't know if it's very good, but it's stuck.
turns.zh:
如今Spotify规模如此之大，以至于其在不同地区的运营方式和产品开发流程都各具特色。多年前——大概12年前——我曾无意间创造了一个产品开发流程模型，当时我们在讨论产品所处的阶段。当时我们急需一个清晰的定义，于是我随口说道："产品开发分为四个阶段：构思、开发、上线和优化。"  

在构思阶段，成本应该尽可能低，不需要投入大量资金。进入开发阶段后，资金投入会大幅增加。因此，必须在构思阶段就降低风险，确保方向正确。随后，产品上线后，再进行持续优化。虽然这个模型并非深思熟虑之作，但有趣的是，我至今仍会听到其他公司提及类似说法，比如"我们正处于构思阶段"或"我们进入了优化阶段"。可见这个模型已深入人心了。虽然我不确定它是否真的科学，但它确实流传开来了。
